speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These changes have been towards a more progressive, balanced and modern criminal justice system that protects society from crime.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And in 2015, the Government began funding criminal legal aid, through the Law Society.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The amendments in these Bills continue in this spirit.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, the presumption of innocence must be respected.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Second, there must be fair processes – they must reflect a balance between various interests and each society must decide for itself what a fair balance is.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Third, accurate outcomes – the system must be effective at arriving at the truth to ensure that the guilty are held accountable and the innocent are not convicted.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The current amendments are made with the same principles in mind.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We made a sustained effort to obtain and consider feedback.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Public consultation was held for a month in July to August 2017.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We received around 30 contributions from a wide spectrum of society: the general public, civil society organisations, banks, technology companies and the Bar.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We also had extensive dialogue with the Law Society and the Criminal Bar from the start of the public consultation until January this year when we had a dialogue with the Criminal Bar and then we took on board a number of their suggestions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Law Society President, Mr Gregory Vijayendran, acknowledged this in his address at the Opening of the Legal Year 2018 when he said, "The Bar appreciates the constructive consultations we have had with the Ministry of Law on amendments to the Criminal Procedure Code.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Law Ministry officials have shown considerable respect for the Law Society's perspectives, a number of which were accommodated.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Even when we agreed to disagree, the process was positive and the dialogue, candid." Finally, there were on-going consultations with the Judiciary, the Attorney-General's Chambers and other Ministries.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There was broad support for the amendments proposed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I would add that we are, concurrently, in the midst of a fairly fundamental review of the Penal Code.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Penal Code Review Committee comprises representatives from the Judiciary, AGC, Criminal Bar, academia and the Government.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The proposed changes to criminal procedure that we are discussing, taken together with the proposed changes to the Penal Code, will put our criminal justice system on a strong footing going forward.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The amendments can be split into three main categories.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Under these three categories, there are more than 50 discrete proposals.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I will not go through the technical amendments in detail, although Members are welcome to ask questions, but I will briefly cover the non-technical amendments.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Let us start with "Investigative Processes" and the introduction of video recording of interviews (VRI).

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Under the current law, law enforcement agencies taking statements under the CPC can only do so in writing.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Bill will allow such statements to be taken via video recording.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This will assist the Courts to try cases more effectively when investigation statements are sought to be admitted in a criminal trial.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, they will be able to take into account the interviewee's demeanour when deciding on the weight to be accorded to statements.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Second, video-recordings also provide an objective account of the interview, to assist the Court in deciding on any allegations made about the conduct of the interview.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The implementation of VRI requires significant investment of infrastructure and training.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It will, therefore, have to be implemented in phases.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, we recognise that there may be instances where there is a need for exceptions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, there may be a need to record a handwritten contemporaneous statement from an accused person at the scene of the crime, when the person is arrested at the scene.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The legislation allows for flexibility to take into account such operational exigencies.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The next set of amendments relate to the powers of investigation relating to evidence stored on computers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Crimes increasingly involve the use of computers, smartphones and the Internet.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We are enhancing the computer-related powers of investigation in the CPC to keep pace with this evolving environment.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Investigators will be able to order the production of evidence stored on computers where such evidence is in the subject's possession or power.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Our investigators have also been analysing and searching through large amounts of data.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: To increase investigators' efficiency when processing electronic evidence produced under such an order, the amendments will allow regulations to be made to specify how such production orders must be complied with, including the format of the reply and the method of delivery.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is intended to enable electronic replies in machine-processable formats.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have consulted industry stakeholders who provide data to our investigators and have taken into account their feedback in determining the requirements that will be imposed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Investigators will also be empowered to access, secure and safeguard evidence on computers, regardless of whether the evidence is stored on a computer inside or outside Singapore.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Many people now use web-based email accounts or web storage accounts.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Technically, such data may reside in computers outside Singapore, even if the data is accessed from within Singapore.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Applicable laws in other countries will be duly considered when such powers are exercised.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Next, on to the search of women suspects.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Bill makes a small but important amendment to the search powers of Police officers and immigration officers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Currently, women can only be searched by female officers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This will allow searches of women suspected of being terrorists where time is of the essence and any delay could mean loss of lives.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Minister for Law had said in late 2014 that the Ministry would be reviewing the framework on bail.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This was after the 2014 hostage-taking incident in a Sydney café perpetrated by a person who was accused of a serious crime and, yet, had been released on bail.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He went on to take 17 innocent persons hostage in a Sydney café.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The incident eventually led to the death of two innocent persons.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There is a need to strike a balance.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On the one hand, the presumption of innocence means that it would be unfair for someone accused of a crime to be kept locked up in remand when he or she has not yet been found guilty by a Court.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But on the other hand, there must be sufficient means to secure the accused person's continued attendance in Court, to ensure justice is served.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The system must also ensure that those who may pose a danger to public safety, are at risk of re-offending while on bail, or who may interfere with evidence, are not released on bail.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With these considerations in mind, the Bill strengthens the bail regime in a number of ways.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, the Bill makes certain adjustments to the categorisation of "bailable" and "non-bailable" offences.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It may be helpful if I clarify for Members the meaning of "bailable" and "non-bailable" at this point, to avoid confusion.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If an offence is “bailable”, it means that the accused person is entitled to bail as of right and if the Prosecution objects, then it is for the Prosecution to show why the person should not be granted bail.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If an offence is "non-bailable", on the other hand, the accused person is not entitled to bail.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He or she must show the Court why bail ought to be granted.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If they fail to do so, they will be remanded.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In practice, many accused persons charged with "non-bailable" offences are released on bail with conditions intended to ensure their attendance in Court.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This brings cheating in line with the treatment of other similar offences carrying similar penalties, for example, criminal breach of trust (CBT).

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Offences which concern false evidence and offences against public justice will also be made non-bailable.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These offences relate to interference with the administration of justice.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Second, the Courts' powers relating to bail and personal bonds will be clarified and enhanced.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, important bail or bond conditions, such as to surrender travel documents or to surrender to custody when required, will be imposed by default unless the Court orders otherwise.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Many of these conditions are, in fact, already ordered by the Court as a matter of course, but this will further tighten the system.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This will assist the Police in monitoring accused persons who have been released on bail.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Court will be given the discretion to withhold bail for bailable offences punishable with imprisonment, if there are substantial grounds to believe that the accused person would abscond.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The rules on execution of bail pending a bail review will be tightened.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If the State Courts grant bail for a non-bailable offence and the Prosecution intends to apply to the High Court for a review of bail, the State Courts will be required to order that the accused person is not allowed to go on bail until the review is determined.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In other words, the accused person will have to be remanded until the High Court decides on the bail review.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If the State Courts grant bail for a bailable offence and the Prosecution intends to apply for review, the State Courts will have a discretion on whether to allow the accused person to go on bail pending determination of the review.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I now move on to Court procedure and evidence and the proposed amendments for enhancing protection for victims of sexual and child abuse offences.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In the past two years or so, there has been a concerted effort to ensure that vulnerable victims of crime are sufficiently protected by our criminal justice system.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: One particularly vulnerable group of victims are those who are subject to sexual or child abuse.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have re-examined every step in the system, to minimise the trauma that such victims experience in the process of bringing perpetrators to justice.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Some measures have already been implemented by the Police, for example, the one-stop centre for medical examinations to minimise waiting time for sexual crime victims, enhanced training curriculum for Police officers to better handle sexual crime cases and the pilot of a Multi-Disciplinary Interview (MDI) model for children who had been sexually abused.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These Bills introduce a suite of measures to further enhance protection.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: One of the fears that victims have when deciding whether to report sexual offences is that media coverage will cause them further distress.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is why the Courts often grant gag orders to prevent the publication of information that may lead to the identification of a victim.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, the case must be before the Court before such an order can be granted.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This means that if a person gets wind of the identity of a victim and the case has not yet come before the Courts, under current law, that person can make public information revealing the victim's identity.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Some suspects may even do this to intimidate the victim and make them basically pay a price for making a Police report.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: To prevent this, the Bill will move the restrictions upstream.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, for example, a person could have confided in a colleague that she was the victim of a sexual offence.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If this colleague makes public the fact that the person was such a victim, the colleague would be committing an offence.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And this applies, even if the person has not reported the offence to the Police.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They will not be allowed to ask questions about the victim's sexual behaviour with persons other than the accused, where such behaviour does not relate to the charge, unless they have leave of Court.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Application for leave must be made in the absence of the victims.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This will help prevent a re-occurrence of the incident that the press reported on late last year, where a defence lawyer embarked on a line of distressing questions when cross-examining an alleged victim of molestation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Testifying in Court can be a difficult experience for such victims.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Where possible, we want to minimise the trauma that these victims face in the Court process.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This will only be implemented in later phases.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We recognise that this must be implemented sensitively in order to help arrive at the truth and we will work with stakeholders on training and methods.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Next, the Courts' discretion to order exceptions to open Court proceedings.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Bill also makes amendments to the State Courts Act and the Supreme Court of Judicature Act, to fine-tune the Courts' discretion to order exceptions to open Court proceedings.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: What we are doing is to clarify the scope of the discretion by setting out a non-exhaustive list of matters that the Court may consider when deciding whether to grant such an order.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, we are not amending the discretion per se; we are just setting out a list of non-exhaustive matters that the Court can take into account.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will also expressly allow the Court to exclude the general public while permitting certain categories of persons to be present, for example, bona fide representatives of the press or media, the families of the victim or accused person, or other persons as the Court may identify in its discretion.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Next, enhancing and rationalising the fitness to plead/unsoundness of mind regime.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The law provides for special procedures to deal with two categories of accused persons with special needs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, those who are "unfit to plead", in other words, not capable of making their defence at the time of trial; and second, those who are acquitted on the basis that they were of unsound mind at the time that they committed the offences.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The procedures balance the need to ensure that such persons are not a danger to themselves or others and the need to respect the fact that such persons have not been convicted of any offence.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They are also designed to provide such persons with the best possible opportunities of recovery, in a controlled environment.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Bills make quite significant amendments to this regime, to allow the Courts and medical professionals to play a more involved role in determining the most appropriate action to take in respect of such persons.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, such persons may be released with certain conditions where they are not assessed to be a danger to themselves or others.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There is a risk in doing this; we have seen instances in other countries where release has led to harm.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, it was reported in 2016 that a man in New Zealand who killed a person but was acquitted on the basis of insanity was released after a few years in detention and, then, had gone on to commit another violent attack in a train station.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, there are these considerations, but it is the right thing to do where doing so would help the accused person’s recovery.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The alternative would be to confine them for extended periods of time, which may not be necessary or helpful.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Due weight will be given to medical opinion, and the necessary conditions imposed, to minimise the risk of re-offending as much as possible.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: A maximum duration will be set for confinements pursuant to the Minister’s orders.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Courts and medical professionals will be given a greater role in supervising such persons and determining what measures to take with respect to such accused persons.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: An accused person released under these CPC provisions may still, however, be subject to detention under the Mental Health (Care and Treatment) Act if he or she is assessed to remain a danger to himself or herself, or to others.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This gives Prosecutors another tool to more effectively deal with corporate offending.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This tool is particularly useful where prosecution of a corporate offender unnecessarily punishes not just the management, but also the employees and shareholders of the corporate entity for what might be the acts of a small number of employees or officers of the company.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The corporation must be represented by counsel and the framework will only apply to scheduled offences.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Such conditions can include: admission of wrongdoing by the corporate offender; and requiring the corporation to pay a financial penalty.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Unlike some criminal fines, the financial penalty will not be subject to a statutory maximum.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: One reason for this is that the harm brought about by corporate offending may eclipse any pre-determined statutory maximum that may be prescribed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Approval will only be granted if the High Court is satisfied that the DPA is in the interests of justice; and its terms are fair, reasonable and proportionate.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Our intention is that in assessing the proportionality of the conditions proposed, the High Court will balance the extent of the wrongdoing, including the revenue or profits attributable to the wrongdoing, with the ability of the corporation to comply.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: To ensure transparency, DPAs must be published after High Court approval unless the Court orders otherwise.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Currently, almost every change in Court procedure, even on technical issues, needs to be tabled in Parliament.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The responsibility for making Court-related procedural rules, for example, timelines for filing documents, will be shifted to the CPRC.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This will allow for Court procedures to remain nimble and up-to-date and is the practice in other countries, such as the United Kingdom.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Besides the Chief Justice who will chair the Committee, the Committee will consist of representatives from the Judiciary, Attorney-General’s Chambers, the Government and the Bar.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As a safeguard, any rule made by the CPRC will have to be approved by both the Chief Justice and the Minister.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have discussed this proposal with the Courts and they are supportive.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Streamlining pre-trial procedures in the High Court and extending the transmission procedure to replace the committal hearing procedure.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Under the present law, cases triable in the High Court must first go through a procedure called a Committal Hearing, before the case is put before the High Court.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The only exception would be serious sexual offences, such as rape, which are transmitted to the High Court by the Public Prosecutor’s fiat.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Historically, this procedure was meant to filter out cases where the Prosecution does not have sufficient evidence to justify a High Court trial.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Such cases are filtered out in two ways: first, the Prosecution is required to disclose the evidence that it has on hand before trial; second, the Defence is allowed to cross-examine the Prosecution’s witnesses to test the evidence.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Today, the main benefit of this procedure has become the pre-trial documentary disclosure, as the Defence seldom chooses to cross-examine Prosecution witnesses.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Doing away with the Committal Hearing will shorten the time that the accused has to spend in remand pending trial.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: A similar review in England and Wales a few years ago also resulted in the abolition of Committal Hearings there.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will continue to require the Prosecution to disclose its case and evidence, in accordance with the criminal disclosure regime, for most cases that today would have been subject to the Committal Hearing procedure.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On the whole, abolishing the Committal Hearing and substituting it with the transmission procedure and criminal disclosure obligations will shorten the waiting time for trial and free up precious judicial resources to focus on the substance of cases.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Extending video link hearings to pleas of guilty and sentencing.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Currently, the law provides for remanded accused persons to appear before the Court through video link for various procedural matters.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This reduces the security risk of transporting remandees between prison and the Courts.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We are expanding the use of video links to hearings for the taking of pleas and sentencing hearings in the State Courts.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The use of video links for such hearings is already in practice in countries, such as the UK, Canada and some states in the US and Australia.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Video links will not be used for trials and judges will retain discretion on whether the accused should be physically produced in Court.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: To provide operational flexibility, the Minister will be able to prescribe other proceedings, both procedural and substantive, in which the accused person may appear before the Court through video link, if remanded at the time of the proceeding.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: MinLaw is working with MHA and the State Courts to pilot this for selected cases in the later part of this year.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will evaluate the experience of using video links for such hearings before extending the procedure.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Next, expanding the Criminal Case Disclosure (CCD) procedure to cover more offences.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Pre-trial disclosure was introduced in the CPC in 2010 as one of the most major changes to criminal procedure in the history of our criminal justice system.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Disclosure has been welcomed and both Prosecutors and Defence counsel have grown comfortable with the system of disclosure.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is, therefore, an opportune time to expand the pre-trial disclosure requirements to more offences.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In recent years, the Courts have seen a rise in the use of psychiatric expert evidence in criminal cases.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Most of the psychiatrists who give evidence are objective and professional.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, there are a few instances where such evidence has fallen short of the basic standards of objectivity and competence expected of expert witnesses.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In one case, the Chief Justice had this to say about the psychiatrist who had given evidence: “not only was the report patently lacking in objectivity, it was plainly erroneous... experts owe their duty first and foremost to the Court and not to the client who pays their fee...” The Bills will require that psychiatrists be admitted to a Court-administered panel of psychiatrists, before they can be called upon to give expert evidence in Court.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This will safeguard the objectivity and quality of psychiatric expert evidence.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have discussed this approach with the Courts, and they are supportive.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We also took in feedback from the Criminal Bar on two practical areas: one, we will formulate the selection criteria to ensure that there is a sufficient pool of psychiatrists available; and two, procedures for the ad hoc admission of foreign psychiatrists will be put in place so that Defence counsel can call such psychiatrists as expert witnesses in appropriate circumstances.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I move on now to sentencing and other powers of the Court.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The introduction of community sentences in 2010 was widely welcomed by members of this House and by stakeholders in the criminal justice system.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have monitored the use of community sentences ─ they have been popular and have worked well in targeting the root causes of crime.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: When implemented well and for suitable cases, community sentences can give those who commit minor offences a good chance at rehabilitation without unnecessary disruption to their lives.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He was diagnosed with Major Depressive Disorder at the Institute of Mental Health (IMH).

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He was subsequently placed under a Mandatory Treatment Order (MTO) for two years.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This entailed regular consultations with his psychiatrist and he was given anti-depressants.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: His sister was also supportive; in fact, he moved in with his sister so that she could provide closer monitoring.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The case manager also followed up regularly to provide counselling.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: His treatment was, therefore, a combination of pharmaceutical and psycho-social care.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Patient A remained offence-free throughout the MTO period and succeeded in completing his Pharmacy degree.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He continued seeing his psychiatrist at IMH after the MTO to continue treatment.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Things could have turned out very differently for this young man, if he had been sentenced to imprisonment.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: While our rehabilitative programmes have grown in sophistication over the years, being cut off from his supportive family network and the disruption to his studies may have undermined his successful rehabilitation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is because of cases like this, that we see value in expanding the eligibility criteria for community sentences, so that more offenders can benefit from the rehabilitative opportunities offered by community sentences.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This will have to be done in a controlled manner, to strike the right balance with deterring crime.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is up from the current availability of MTOs only for offences punishable with up to three years’ imprisonment.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This will allow the IMH to deliver a more effective treatment programme, where needed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The suspended sentence will take effect the moment a community sentence has been breached.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This will encourage compliance with community sentences, when imposed in suitable cases.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Besides community sentences, the Bills also make major changes to another sentencing option that is focused on rehabilitation – the reformative training (RT) regime.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The RT regime is specifically geared towards the rehabilitation of young offenders.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It emphasises both discipline and rehabilitation in a structured environment, where officers provide supervision and guidance to the RT trainees.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The trainees will go through programmes that will help them take charge of their rehabilitation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They will need to soberly reflect on their offences, how to stay crime-free and strengthen their relationships with their family.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The RT regime has been an important and effective one but we are always striving to see how we can improve.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Over the years of running the reformative training regime, the Singapore Prison Service (SPS) has gained a deeper understanding of evidence-based rehabilitation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The proposed changes reflect this deeper understanding, allowing SPS to take on a risk – and performance-based approach in determining the intensity of intervention in RTC for the trainee.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This will be based on the time required for programming to mitigate the risks and address the needs of the RT trainees, according to their profiles.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The amendments, hence, allow for a more nuanced assessment of the intensity of rehabilitation required, depending on each individual's likely response to RT and level of motivation to change.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Currently, trainees are already grouped by risk profile and rehabilitation needs, where they undergo rehabilitation in an environment that minimises contamination.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Currently, trainees are already provided with opportunities for education and skills training while in detention.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The new minimum detention periods mean that disruption, if any, to education will be further reduced.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For some of the trainees, they can pursue their educational goals on supervision in the community as early as the sixth-month mark.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Despite the changes, it is important to emphasise that the purposes of RT have not changed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It achieves the sentencing objectives of rehabilitation and deterrence.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It offers the Courts an option to rehabilitate the offender in a structured environment while achieving deterrence.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: RT will continue to be the preferred option for cases where the need for rehabilitation corresponds with the need for heightened deterrence.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It should ordinarily be imposed on repeat offenders or for serious offences like drug trafficking.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Each case should, however, be treated on its own facts and there may be exceptions where RT is unsuitable due to the characteristics of the offender or the heinous nature of the offence committed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: New procedures to prevent abuse of Court process in concluded criminal cases.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have looked at the procedure set out by the Court of Appeal and we agree that it strikes the right balance between preventing miscarriages of justice and the need for finality in criminal proceedings where all appeals have already been exhausted.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Courts' powers to order compensation in the CPC recognise that criminal law is not just about the public’s interests but also about the interests of individual victims.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: MinLaw has been looking at ways to make the victim compensation regime more effective.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In 2010, we made it mandatory for the Court to consider in every case whether it should order compensation.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Senior Minister of State, can we pause for a while.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Dragging out proceedings to deal with compensation will have a knock-on effect on the Court’s ability to deal with other cases.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They keep pace with the evolving values of society and with international best practices.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: An effective criminal justice system is important in a rule-of-law country.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Those who obey the law must be confident that they will not be wrongly convicted and punished.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Beyond that, the criminal justice system has to retain its legitimacy of addressing injustices so that people will not turn to vigilante acts.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For this legitimacy to be maintained, the criminal justice system must be concerned with arriving at the correct outcome and arriving at it in a fair and impartial manner.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: After all, "a person is innocent until proven guilty".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The evidence-gathering process would, hence, become more transparent and there can be no allegations of the statement not being read back in a language the accused is familiar with.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As such, the accused may perceive this as a fairer process.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Before I go on to the next part of my speech, I should make a declaration that I am a legal practitioner, practising both civil and criminal law.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By being able to look over the statements before the trial, the defence will be able to identify and home in on the key disputes.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By having access to more information, the defence would be able to better prepare a more accurate case in the adversarial system, thereby promoting a more precise outcome.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I also want to highlight two other amendments in light of this rationale of fairness.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With regard to protecting vulnerable victims, a balance has to be struck between removing barriers that deter a victim from taking the perpetrator to task and ensuring that the process remains fair to the accused.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In order to secure a rightful conviction, the victim often needs to testify.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Testifying to the hideous acts that have been done can be a very daunting and harrowing experience, especially if done in full view of the perpetrator.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By providing for video-recorded statements to be adduced as verbal evidence, it reduces the need to recount the traumatic experiences again and again.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would the Minister clarify how this will be done operationally; in particular, would the statement be recorded by a third-party person in authority and would the person giving the statement know, while giving the statement that it would be used in a Court proceeding?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The new section 281B accords some certainty of protection when a victim needs to testify to the harrowing details of the alleged offence.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Through it, he or she will be able to give evidence in-camera, if he or she wishes to.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While this would reduce the pressure of giving testimony in a public setting, the public interest in the publicity of criminal proceedings will still be served through the amendments in clauses 126 and 127 which would give the Court the discretion to allow journalists and individuals with sufficient interest to attend in-camera proceedings.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hopefully, the names of the vulnerable victims or witnesses will be concealed.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even as we seek to remove obstacles from victims seeking redress through the proper channel, we must also bear in mind the tenet of "innocent until proven guilty".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, we need to take a balanced and measured approach.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, when it comes to the evidential shield in the Evidence (Amendment) Bill that prevents a defence counsel from asking certain questions without Court approval, we must make sure that it will not interfere with a fair trial – a right of the accused – in an adversarial system.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The right of the accused who is innocent until proven guilty in such an adversarial system.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Allow me to turn to the restriction of psychiatrist experts to a panel, which is done through the new section 270.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The rules of eligibility have to be carefully crafted so that it will be grounded on the objectivity of a psychiatrist's testimony and not add pressure on the psychiatrist to favour one side or the other.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In this regard, I would like to seek a clarification as to the purpose for the two-year term in subsection (2) as well as the possibility for revocation under subsection (4).

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Additionally, by limiting the supply of such experts, fees may increase.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By limiting who can testify in Court on such evidence, this places a limitation on what a defence counsel may do to present his most accurate case.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, to ensure the rationale of fairness remains paramount in the trial process, we should have, in my view, a long panel list of psychiatrist experts and not restrict the panel to a short list.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This will allow a mentally-ill accused person to see a medical professional he or she is most comfortable with.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the same vein, I would like to seek a clarification regarding clause 74.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The explanatory statement paragraph (b) of the relevant portion, says this: "by inserting new subsection (4A) to clarify that the making of a statement by an accused is not to be regarded as caused by any inducement, threat or promise merely because a person in authority had earlier informed the accused that the accused was required or legally bound to give information under section 27 of the Prevention of Corruption Act (PCA) (Cap 241), if that person believed any of certain things in good faith, when so informing the accused." Big mouthful; I will get to my point.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Previously, however, in Annex B, and I quote: "Table of Proposed Legislative Changes to the Criminal Procedure Code (CPC) and the Evidence Act" used for public consultation, item 29 says that "It has been stated in previous Court decisions that telling an interviewee that he is bound to tell the truth in respect of non-corruption offences can amount to inducement, which renders a statement inadmissible.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is because section 27 of the PCA only applies to offences under the PCA.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Moving on, Sir, the criminal justice system needs to be fair and it needs to be fair for everyone who may find themselves in that system, not just the rich but, importantly, the poor.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Moving on, a criminal justice system needs to be fair and, in administering justice, the decisions have to be accurate and equitable.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Upon conviction, different principles and considerations comein to play.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These are just some of the important questions that have to be considered in the drafting of the post-conviction portion of the CPC.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To this end, I welcome the expansion of the community-based sentencing regime.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Community-based sentencing seeks to put rehabilitation at the centre of the sentence.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For some orders, there is less disruption to social support around the offender.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This can be seen even for the Mandatory Treatment Order, where there is a possibility of a family or a friend taking care of the offender.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Community-based sentencing would also make it easier to maintain gainful employment and be less disruptive to studies for younger offenders.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because of this, community-based sentencing ameliorates some difficulties of reintegration.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It also supports rehabilitation efforts by allowing an individual to remain in the community.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This Bill expands the scope of community-based sentencing to cover more offences and offenders and I hope that this will further promote the effective reduction of crimes through rehabilitation while, at the same time, not diluting a consistent message of deterrence, for deterrence is also an important rationale in sentencing.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another amendment that deals with post-conviction considerations head-on is straightening the framework of victim compensation under the CPC.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As the Singapore High Court in Soh Meiyun v Public Prosecutor said, "Compensation Orders are, in effect a shortcut to the remedy that the victim could obtain in a civil suit against the offender".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is especially important when a victim does not have the financial means to initiate a civil suit and yet requires the same compensation as those who can, especially compensation for medical bills as a result of an offender's actions.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As they have an interest in the matter, the provision also gives standing to the person being compensated to adduce evidence and make submissions.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That is, "  should not require the Court to embark on complicated investigations of fact or law", taken from the leaf of the judgment of Soh Meiyun v Public Prosecutor at paragraph 58.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This Bill does not just make it mandatory for the trial judge to consider victim compensation but also makes it mandatory for the trial judge to give reasons as to why he or she does not make such an order.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To be fair to the accused who may have difficulty paying such compensation amounts as well, subsection 2B of section 359 will make it explicit that the Court must consider the offender's financial means and subsection 2C will empower the Court to make a financial circumstances order to establish this.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: When it comes to corporations, the Deferred Prosecution Scheme seeks to resolve systemic problems in corporations that led to the offence being committed in the first place, for example, through requiring certain processes to be set in place.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It also seeks to resolve the difficulties in punishing the legal personality or the separate legal personality of a company.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It does this by facilitating investigations so that there can be a more meaningful attribution of culpability.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There is, therefore, a strict requirement that it must be a corporation or association that is represented by an advocate.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Is that advocate required to be a practising member of the bar?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: While I agree that the Bill carries important and progressive reforms, I do not think it is possible for any law to ensure correct and equitable outcomes in the criminal justice system.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: There will always be a risk of the innocent being convicted, the guilty being acquitted and victims being left without redress even with the best laws in place.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Nevertheless, I do welcome the significant reforms being made to the CPC to give greater assurance of good and fair outcomes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: In my speech, I will first highlight what I see as enhancements to the law, after which I will articulate some concerns which I believe the Ministry should address.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The Bill has rightly slaughtered some longstanding and sacred cows.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: This is something which practitioners, including myself, have called for over the last 10 years as this is an important safeguard, not just for the accused person but also beneficial for the state.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Based on experiences in other countries, a video-recording will not only give some protection to the accused person from giving statements under pressure or duress, but it will also reduce the likelihood of frivolous allegations being made against investigators which, in turn, will save Court time.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I presume that, in future, other offences will be added to the Third Schedule for compulsory video-recording.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Clauses 6 and 7 also provide for video-recording of accused statements as an option in other cases besides rape if the Police officer or forensic specialist so decides.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The Bill, however, is silent on what circumstances the Police officer or forensic specialist is to take into account before deciding that a video-recorded statement should be taken.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I would like some clarification from the Ministry on this.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: In the last major CPC review, a Statutory Framework was introduced for the prosecution and the defence to disclose to each other the key details, witnesses and exhibits long before trial.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I believe the CCD regime has worked well over the last few years to promote fair trials and also to build trust between the prosecution and defence.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The Bill now extends this regime to cover offences under several additional laws, including the PCA, something I had asked about previously.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The move to include more legislation under the Disclosure regime will build more confidence in the system.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Thirdly, the rights of crime victims are being further enshrined in the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Traditional criminal justice systems do not focus on the victim as the parties to a criminal case are the state and the accused person, with the crime victim reduced to being a prosecution witness, with no redress for harm suffered.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Across the world, developed countries recognised this gap and promoted studies and victimology, putting in place reforms on matters, such as reducing victim trauma during investigations and in Court, and providing victim support.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: In this Bill, clause 98 will further amend section 359 of the CPC significantly, by requiring judges who do not make Compensation Orders for victim injuries to record the reasons why they did not do so.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: This is a strong signal from Parliament, which I expect to greatly increase the numbers of Compensation Orders made.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: After listening to the long and detailed Second Reading speech from the Senior Minister of State, I would like, today, to just focus on two of these changes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: First, the introduction of Deferred Prosecution Agreements (DPA) and secondly, the extension of video-link usage under clause 80.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: DPAs have been in use in other jurisdictions, such as the USA and the UK.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I agree that DPAs are important tools to address corporate crime as they enable the state to incentivise corporations to fully investigate and cooperate with the authorities.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Such cooperation would also save time and resources for the state as it facilitates the state having access to information from within the corporations more efficiently.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The DPA scheme introduced by this Bill enables flexible and customised resolutions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The offending corporation may be required to compensate victims, donate monies to a charity, implement compliance and training programmes and appoint auditors to monitor progress of remedial measures.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Notwithstanding the virtues of DPAs, the fact remains that the DPA is an avenue by which a corporation which has committed a serious offence can avoid prosecution and conviction.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: This is a consequence that is of tremendous benefit to a corporation in that it will not have a conviction recorded against it, which will, in turn, allow it to continue business and not face consequences, such as being blacklisted or debarred from projects.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Thus, the circumstances under which DPAs are offered and entered are of immense public interest.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: It is stated that the High Court must find that the DPA is in the interest of justice and that the terms of the DPA are fair, reasonable and proportionate.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: However, what needs closer scrutiny is that the Bill seems to require less disclosure of the Court's considerations than, say, the scheme in the UK.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: In the UK, DPAs are regulated under Schedule 17 of the UK's Crime and Courts Act which stipulates that the Crown Court must give reasons in open Court for why it has approved a DPA in the interests of justice and why it considers the terms of the DPA to be fair, reasonable and proportionate.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: After all, entering a DPA is a big deal in the sense that the state is agreeing to let a corporation avoid prosecution for a serious offence that it admits to committing.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: This option of entering a DPA is not available to all offenders but is selectively applied and not applicable to individual offenders.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, how corporations are chosen, the considerations for imposing certain conditions on the corporations and the approved methods of monitoring the corporations for compliance will be of public interest.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: In my view, making it mandatory for the High Court to publicly justify why it approved a DPA can only help to instill confidence in the system.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I am concerned about clause 80 on the use of video-link for Court proceedings.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I do not have any issue with the changes allowing vulnerable victims to testify in Court via video link in certain types of cases as this will likely reduce the victim's trauma in Court.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: However, I am concerned about the further extension of video-link communications with accused persons who are remanded in prison while their cases are pending.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Under the current section 281(3) of the CPC, an accused may appear via video link if the Court is considering applications for release on bail or bond after the first mention and in proceedings for extension of remand and in such other matters that may be prescribed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I am not aware of any other matters currently being prescribed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: If passed, this will mean that there will be no need for the Prisons to arrange to bring an accused out of prison to Court in order that his plea, conviction and sentence be dealt with face-to-face between the Court and the accused.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: From the Court's point of view, at the time of conviction and sentence, we often see judges admonishing accused persons or warning them not to repeat their behaviour or face more serious consequence in future.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Will the effect of such warnings be diminished if seen through a TV screen?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: As for the defence, the stage of the accused pleading guilty and being sentenced is a critical one where counsel will usually need to confer with his accused in detail.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Such communications would include checking with the accused person on the correctness of the statement of facts prepared by the prosecution, which would, in turn, have a direct impact on the sentence imposed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Counsel may also need to take his client's instructions if the prosecution objects to any part of the defence's mitigation plea and also seek client's instructions on the prosecution's sentencing positions, which may only be communicated on the day of the hearing to take a guilty plea.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Where video link is used, the defence counsel will be in Court while his client is in prison.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Nevertheless, there are some aspects, such as those I have highlighted, that required further attention.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In introducing this proposed Bill, the Minister for Law has stated that the purpose of this Bill is to enhance the fairness of existing procedures and to ensure the accuracy and equity of the outcomes in the criminal justice system.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: To this end, amendments, such as the introduction of video-recordings of the statement of suspects who have allegedly committed rape offences as well as to prevent defence lawyers from questioning complaints of sexual and child abuse offences on their past sexual history and behaviours, are aligned with the principles outlined by the Minister and are most welcomed.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The NGOs I spoke to welcomed the introduction of video-recording of the suspect’s statement as a step towards reducing the incidents of false or involuntary confessions arising from threat, inducement or promise.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: However, a few concerns were raised as to whether the present amendments sufficiently protect the integrity and evidentiary value of a suspect's statements taken via audio-visual recording.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Other safeguards must also be put in place to ensure that the video-recording does not give a misrepresented picture of the suspect's demeanour or interfere with the evidential value of the recording.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: One such safeguard is to ensure that the entire interrogation process or interactions between the Police and the suspect be recorded on video.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In situations where the threat, inducement and/or promise may have been communicated to the suspect prior to the taking of the audio-visual recording, but are not recorded, the purpose of video-recording of the statement of the suspect is defeated.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Another instance, if there have already been multiple rounds of pre-questioning and interrogation prior to the taking of the audio-visual recording, research studies have shown that the suspect might appear far more callous and unremorseful when their statements are taken via video-recording thereafter.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: As such, the recording of the suspect's statement after such intensive interrogations may not provide the Court with an accurate picture of the suspect's demeanour or his voluntariness in making such a statement.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, there are several technical aspects of the conduct of the video-recording that, if not undertaken, may compromise the accuracy in the assessment of the demeanour of the suspect.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Consider a situation where the video frame is focused only on the suspect’s face and not on his other body parts.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The suspect’s facial movements on camera may suggest that he is calm but his body movements may suggest that the suspect is operating under distress but such signs of distress may not be captured on video-recording.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, under such circumstances, we may not be capturing the accurate assessment of the suspect's demeanour or make a finding as to whether the statement was made by the suspect voluntarily.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is also important that safeguards be in place to ensure that the video footage will not be tempered or ill-edited such that important or material portions of the audio-visual recording are inadvertently cut-off and not provided to the defence.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I also hope that the Ministry will continue to expand the scope of offences where video-recording of statements, especially for serious offences which carry severe punishments, such as life imprisonment and capital punishment.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I will look at clauses 6 and 77 of the Bill which permit the recording of a statement from a vulnerable victim.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I am heartened to see that the Government is taking such steps to protect the interests of vulnerable victims and to support them through the investigation process.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that investigators are now allowed to take statements from such vulnerable victims via video-recording and that the video-recorded witness statement scheme will be implemented in stages.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I have two points to raise on this scheme.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The second point which I want to raise pertains to a concern which AWARE raised in its submission on this specific video-recording scheme of the statements of vulnerable victims of sexual crimes.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Based on AWARE's working experience with vulnerable victims who have been sexually assaulted or abused, many of such victims may be reluctant to speak about their experience out of fear and embarrassment.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The knowledge that they might be filmed while recounting their experience might cause them to feel intimidated or be less willing to share sensitive details via video-recording.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The use of video-recording to record statements of vulnerable victims might potentially be counterproductive to ensuring an accurate assessment of the facts.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: My main concerns with this panel of psychiatrists are whether its implementation will restrict the defence's ability to effectively conduct their defence.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: First, I would like to know if there are any price controls to regulate and ensure that the cost of hiring a psychiatrist from such a panel will not be excessive and will remain affordable to suspects who are financially-strapped.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Second, will the Minister consider permitting an ad hoc admission basis, alongside this scheme, should there be a psychiatrist whose expertise may be very relevant in assisting the Court but who may not be able to meet the admission criteria?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I am glad just now to hear from the Senior Minister of State that it would have such ad hoc admission for overseas psychiatrists.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I am sure, even if we have this list of psychiatrists no matter how long the list, there will be situations whereby we may need to have to admit some other possibilities.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Third, how will the Ministry ensure that there are sufficient numbers of psychiatrists on the panel such that it will not limit the pool of expert witnesses from which the prosecution or the defence may appoint?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: When this proposal was first introduced in 2017, some doctors had raised concerns on whether the admission criteria may be too stringent and thereby causing psychiatrists to turn away from forensic work, which further reduces the number of psychiatrists who may be appointed to this panel.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: NUS law professor Jeffrey Pinsler has cautioned that the psychiatrist who is on the panel may be unwilling to state his honest but controversial view for fear that he may appear to lack objectivity and lose his place on the panel.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I hope the Senior Minister of State can share with the House what is being done to address these concerns.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: There are two main concerns which I have with this proposed clause.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Years down the road, the applicant comes into possession of new evidence which may potentially prove his innocence.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Such an applicant would be precluded from being able to bring another review application based on the strict wording of section 394K which only permits him to make only one review application which he has already exhausted.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: If such an accused person is able to obtain new material which may prove his innocence, I do not think the law should be so rigid as to not permit such an applicant to re-open his case.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: One of the conditions that the accused must show is that the material cannot be adduced in Court earlier even with reasonable diligence and that the material is credible, substantial, powerfully probative and capable of showing almost conclusively that there has been a miscarriage of justice in the criminal matter in respect of which the earlier decision was made.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: This section is a relatively high threshold standard for accused persons to satisfy in order to re-open their case.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I am worried that such a provision might preclude the accused person who may not be able to meet such threshold but, nonetheless, are able to show evidence that might prove their innocence.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Take, for instance, accused persons who represent themselves.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Without the benefit of legal advice, a self-represented suspect may not know or appreciate that particular evidence or material which he or she possesses may be material or relevant to proving their case and, thereby, did not adduce it when the case was on-going.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Given that a justice system is subject to human fallibility, we should have a justice system that is flexible enough to correct such human errors where they occur.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I, therefore, hope the Minister can reconsider this proposed section 394J and perhaps create an exception under the proposed section to allow meritorious cases.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: For consideration, perhaps such an exception may provide that accused persons who did not intentionally or deliberately not disclose such evidence during the criminal proceeding are not precluded from re-opening a concluded case.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I support this Bill but I hope that the Minister will address the four areas of concerns that I have shared in this House.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But, finally, I would also want to draw attention to the proposed amendment in the Evidence (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I applaud the move to protect victims of sexual offences and child abuse.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In a Straits Times' report about the case of the 36-year-old man sentenced to 16 years for molesting and raping his mother, the report outlined how the defence cross- examined the victim.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: A woman who was a sexual abuse victim, after reading the article, wrote to AWARE to voice her concerns about unrestrained cross-examination.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: She has given permission for me to share her thoughts about what she felt as a victim when reading about that cross-examination.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I will read a portion of her letter.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I quote, "For me, being attacked by someone I loved was confusing and shocking.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: You are trying to make sense of the world to comprehend what the heck just happened, trying to figure out why he did not understand you, how this massive miscommunication just occurred.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Your mind is nowhere near trying to seek revenge or justice.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Going to the Police means getting that person into trouble, and you still love that person.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: And why would you tear up your life even more by going at your family?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I could not bear their concern or worry or anger.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: And till today, it is really hard for me to use the words 'rape' or even, perhaps more accurately, 'forcible sodomy' to describe what happened.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Those words are forceful, heavy, have all sorts of violent and awful connotations.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Just because victims do not use certain words does not mean that what Courts understand that thing to be, did not happen to them.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: And I remember going 'about my usual routine' as well.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I had a lecture to give the next day.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We still have responsibilities to fulfil, jobs to tend to.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Other people's lives do not just ground to a halt because of what happened to you the day before.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I do not know why lawyers, or indeed, people, in this day and age, continue to believe that sexual assault victims must all behave in a certain way after their incidents, or else they must be lying.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But what really concerns me is that these attitudes are brought into Courtrooms.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I do not think I can defend how I behaved after my incident many years ago.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I certainly could not do it while facing a Senior Counsel.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I do not think I could withstand being put on trial for how I behaved after the incident, as if how I behaved had anything to do with how I feel even years after the fact.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I think this Bill is an important step and hope we can continue our effort to protect the victims of sexual offences and child abuse.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I am supportive of the proposed revamp of the criminal procedural rules.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It is laudable that efforts are undertaken to move our criminal justice system toward a more progressive and balanced one.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I have some queries which I would like to raise in relation to some of the changes proposed under the Bill.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: With the introduction of this new mode of taking of statements, how are our Police officers being equipped to take video-recorded statements?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: What training is in place to prepare our Police officers and other support persons involved in the interview process, such as forensic specialists and interpreters, for this new mode of taking statements?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Would a set of guidelines or practice directions be put together to assist the Police officers in achieving the intended outcomes of video-recorded statements?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In putting this set of guidelines together, reference can be made to other jurisdictions' experience in the taking of video-recorded statements.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In 2016, the Australian Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse conducted an evaluation of alternative measures used in eliciting evidence from complainants of child sexual abuse, such as through pre-recorded Police interviews.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It was found that technological problems associated with the use of pre-recorded interviews could impact the trial, delay proceedings, extend trial times and, at times, cause distress to complainants.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: These technological problems include low audio clarity and image clarity and the failure to capture images of the complainant that allowed for an adequate assessment of demeanour, such as by omitting an image of more than just the complainant's face, or by placing the camera at such great distance from the complainant that facial expressions were not adequately displayed.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We can then take reference from these findings and implement measures to ensure such technological issues are mitigated or, where possible, overcomed.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The Australian Royal Commission also found that one of the concerns among the legal practitioners who were interviewed in the study was the quality of Police interviews, which were described as suggestive at times, cluttered with irrelevant details and prone to omitting important evidential details.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It was recommended that there was a need to adopt better guidance and address issues in skills development and quality assurance, to improve Police interview practices.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In the same vein, we can do more to prepare our officers to enhance the quality of Police interviews.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I would also like to seek clarification on the experience of Police officers who take statements which can be used as evidence.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: For example, under the current CPC, statements taken pursuant to section 258(1) of the CPC shall be used in evidence if it is made to a Police officer below the rank of Sergeant.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This has been the rule for some time where, in the past, Sergeants were less likely to be fresh hires and would have had accumulated more experience in the force before rising to the rank of Sergeant.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Today, most of the new hires enter the force as Sergeants or at a higher rank.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Would it be timely to review this rule to ensure that the officers who are taking statements possess adequate experience in the taking of statements for use as evidence?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Second, safeguards to ensure security of video-recorded statements.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: What safeguards are being put in place to ensure that the security of these video-recorded statements is not compromised, such as through hacking or illicit recording of the video-recorded statements?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The Bill allows vulnerable witnesses to use a screen in Court while giving evidence on the stand to prevent him from being seen by the accused.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Once again, we can take a leaf from other jurisdictions' experience in the use of screens in the Courtroom.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The Australian Royal Commission, in their 2016 study, gathered feedback on the use of screens in the Courtroom and found that some defence counsel and judges were of the view that the use of screens was unfair to the accused as he was not able to see the witness who was giving evidence against him.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Some stakeholders also found the use of screens to be ineffective in reducing the witness' stress as the witness was still aware of the proximity of the accused and, in some instances, the accused could still be seen by the witness when the accused moved.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Also, due to the layout of the Courtroom, the witness would often still be seen by the accused as they had to walk past the accused to get to the witness box.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Some Courtrooms also did not utilise well-designed and purpose-built screens, as a result, the use of a screen was viewed as a negative experience for the witness, making the Court process more complex and, at times, unintentionally blocking the view of other members of the Court.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It would be useful if a set of guidelines or practice directions could be put together on the use of screens in the Courtroom to ensure that it is able to achieve its intended purpose.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This is especially in light of the recent case of Chew Eng Han who attempted to flee Singapore while he was out on bail.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: For those who had absconded, were they later apprehended and what happened to these accused persons or convicted persons?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I also note that under the Bill, the Court will now be allowed to grant bail in extradition cases if special circumstances apply.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Under the current bail regime, bail cannot be granted at all for extradition cases.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I am supportive of the establishment of the Criminal Procedure Rules Committee which is conferred the power to prescribe Court-related procedural rules to keep the Court process nimble and up-to-date.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
