text: Besides the 13 members identified in the Bill, I would like to propose that the Committee should also regularly seek inputs from the social science and technology experts to review the criminal procedural rules and identify ways to enhance the robustness and fairness of our criminal justice system.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In respect of having a Court-administered panel of psychiatrists to ensure that evidence given by psychiatrists in Court is competently arrived at and objective, I would like to ask the Minister what selection criteria will be applied to assess if a psychiatrist should be appointed to the panel.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: What safeguards are in place to ensure that the selection criteria do not inadvertently cause the composition of the panel to lack diversity of views which are within the limits of objective opinion?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Are there plans to provide this panel of psychiatrists with training to enable them to better understand Court processes and the role they play in adversarial proceedings, to enable them to be able to perform their role more competently?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: How many offenders have failed to comply with the conditions of their MTO sentences?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: How many offenders re-offend or cause harm to themselves or others during their MTO sentence due to their mental condition?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I would also like to ask the Minister what community-based support does the offender receive during the course of the MTO and what safeguards are put in place to ensure that the victims of these offenders are protected while the offender is allowed to remain in the community to seek treatment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: For example, in a recent case where a woman was given a two-year MTO for harassing her neighbour, the offender continued to harass her neighbours on a daily basis by verbally abusing them and throwing urine and rubbish at her neighbours' premises.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It was reported that such harassment has gone on for years.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In such cases, what can be done to ensure that the victims do not continue to be harassed by the offender as the offender seeks treatment?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: There is a need to provide a support system to ensure that the victims of these offenders are not overlooked as well.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In the United Kingdom, DPAs were introduced in 2014 and, prior to that, the Serious Fraud Office and the Crown Prosecution Service had published a code of practice for the use of DPAs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The code provides guidance on factors that the prosecutor may take into account when deciding whether to enter into a DPA.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Under the Bill, a DPA only comes into force when the High Court approves the DPA by making the relevant declaration.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Upon the High Court making a relevant declaration, the Public Prosecutor must give public notice of the following: (a) the DPA to which the relevant declaration relates; (b) the relevant declaration; (c) the reasons given by the High Court for its decision to make the relevant declaration, if any.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Would the Minister consider making public the reasons given by the High Court in cases where the High Court does not make a relevant declaration?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This will help to ensure consistent and transparent application of the DPA tool.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This will also afford guidance on what cases are best suited for DPA and to provide corporations with more certainty in the management of their affairs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Child abuse and sexual offences are particularly traumatic offences and victims are often afraid to come forward to report the offences due to a variety of reasons, ranging from being unable to make sense of what has happened to them, fear of the perpetrator, fear of judgement and being subjected to further humiliation and shame, fear that they would be blamed for their predicament, fear that they would not be believed and the fear of having to recount and relive the experience repeatedly in the course of investigation and in the adjudication process.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In adversarial proceedings, we can and must ensure that the victim of the offence is, as far as possible, protected from being re-victimised in the cross-examination process.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I am supportive of this move and would like to suggest some ways in which the scope of the amendment could be expanded.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: First, the Bill defines "child abuse offence" and "sexual offence" to mean any offence specified in the First Schedule.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In addition to the sections of the Children and Young Persons Act, Penal Code and the Women’s Charter listed in the First Schedule, should sections 366 and 367 of the Penal Code (Cap 224) be included in the First Schedule as well, given that these sections also deal with offences of a sexual nature?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Besides child abuse and sexual offences, should certain criminal intimidation offences under section 506 of the Penal Code or harassment offences under the Protection from Harassment Act also be treated in the same manner, in particular, where the criminal intimidation imputes unchastity to a woman or where harassment is sexual in nature?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Could the presiding judge be given flexibility to decide to apply similar restrictions on cross-examination to those cases, even though they are not offences listed in the First Schedule?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The guidelines would serve as a guide to help prosecutors and defence counsel put the amendment into practice without diminishing the right of the accused to a fair trial.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I understand that the Law Society is working on a set of guidelines of best practices for examination of children and victims of sexual offences and is aiming to issue the guidelines this year.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In particular, I hope that this set of guidelines would instruct defence counsel to refrain from making baseless submissions that disparage the character, integrity or morality of the victim or premise their case theory on unsubstantiated myths and stereotypes to attempt to shift the blame to the victim.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), the principal public prosecuting agency for conducting criminal prosecutions in England and Wales, has developed a set of Guidelines on Prosecuting Cases of Child Sexual Abuse and have identified a list of myths and stereotypes which should be challenged in Court.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: These myths and stereotypes had been relied on by some defence counsel in representing accused persons in sexual offences before the Singapore Courts.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In defending his client accused of outrage of modesty, defence counsel in Public Prosecutor v Xu Jiadong asked the complainant to stand up in Court to assess her "attractiveness" and suggested to the Court that he would have to know the complainant’s breast size and whether she had been wearing low cut attire on the day of the incident.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The judge found that the defence counsel’s line of questioning was indecent, scandalous and intended to insult or annoy the victim.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Not only were the questions offensive, I find it regrettable that the defence’s case was premised on misogynistic stereotypes that the complainant’s looks and dressing had, in some manner, induced the accused to outrage her modesty.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This is an example of the type of myths and stereotypes which should not be perpetuated.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In the case of Public Prosecutor v BLV, the defence counsel sought to rely on the complainant’s ability to keep her composure at the time of interviews by the medical assessors and the complainant’s good performance in school to indicate her lack of credibility as regards the occurrence of the alleged sexual abuse by her father.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In Ng Jun Xian v Public Prosecutor, the High Court found that it was wholly unnecessary for defence counsel to specifically highlight that the victim was older, was sexually experienced or that she was calm when she was examined by the doctor.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: More recently, in defending the accused who was charged with the rape of his biological mother, defence counsel made the argument that the complainant could have "shut the gates" by crossing her legs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The prosecutor submitted that this line of argument was premised on the antediluvian notion that a woman could resist a rapist if she really wanted to and there was no room for such statements in the 21st century, both in the Court and outside of it.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: While the prosecutors and judges had intervened in the aforementioned cases, the complainants had already been unduly subjected to unnecessary lines of questioning and assertions while being put on the stand.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In respect of cross-examining child witnesses, the Law Society has come up with some draft guidelines on the approach that defence counsel should take when doing so.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Some of these guidelines include adjusting the pace of questioning to the child’s needs, making sure that the child understands the questions posed and ensuring that the defence counsel’s tone of voice and body language are neutral.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Defence counsel should be sensitive to this general rule of practice and the particular circumstances of the witness and calibrate their cross-examination questions accordingly so that they do not inadvertently badger the witness and subject the witness to undue stress in addressing these inconsistencies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It should be explained to the victims that, in the course of cross-examination, defence counsel will put their case to them and the questions posed may be upsetting to them as they seek to make out the elements of the accused's case.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The gist of that speech was that there is no such thing as an unmeritorious prosecution, only an unsuccessful one.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: That was the approach then and I am very happy to say that, from what I have heard and from this particular Bill that is before us, that is not the current mindset of the Ministry.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The Ministry has proposed significant contemporary changes of the criminal justice system.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It marks, in their words, a "major step in the long-term move towards a more progressive, balanced and modern criminal justice system." I celebrate that move, welcome it, and I declare at this point that I am a consultant to the Criminal Practice Committee of the Law Society.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Over the past several months, we have had an opportunity to meet with the Ministry at all levels several times and we have done what lawyers do best – after these consultations, argue.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: We followed up with copious notes and extensive submissions.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: So, I will not go through every point that was raised.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I am just happy to note that quite a few of these points were incorporated in the refinements to the draft Bill at that time.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I will focus on a few points that I think we would like some clarification on, Mr Speaker.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: What that does is that it removes the possibility that evidence was tampered with at an early stage, the statements were coerced through threat, inducement and promise – that is the hope, in time.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But it is good that we at least have the possibility for video-recording now.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I do raise a few points in relation to video-recording in two separate respects.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Is there a reason why a lawyer who has a professional responsibility as an advocate and solicitor not to disclose that recording in public should be not provided this copy?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: If the fear is that a foolish or crooked defence lawyer may disclose the footage, then perhaps could the Ministry require defence counsel to sign an undertaking that they shall not disclose the footage?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: A breach of such an undertaking of course would be on pain of disciplinary penalties and, perhaps, even prosecution.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: So, is there a reason why we would not disclose a video-recording to the defence counsel themselves?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I say this with full knowledge that the defence counsel would have an opportunity to look at the video-recording at the Police station or at a particular place that the Minister so prescribes.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I ask this because, in preparation for the defence's case, viewing footage as to how the long statement and short statement are made, they are the first statements that are given to the Police, are crucial for the preparation of the defence's case, and preparation often cannot be done by just looking at a video-recording once.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: When evidence is led, Mr Speaker, leading questions are not permitted and can be subjected to "on the spot" objections.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But this rule may not be practically enforceable in a video-recorded interview.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The potential of an interviewer inadvertently prejudicing the evidence cannot be ruled out, especially if the interviewer is not a trained advocate.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Will the video be shown in its entirety to a vulnerable complainant?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Where there are breaks in the interview, will these be recorded and shown?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Will the video that is shown in its entirety, if it is, show all the individuals who are present in the room at that time?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: These are nagging questions, Mr Speaker, especially because these are often the questions that are raised by defence counsel.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Now, at the point if there was no video-recording, these are the questions that you will ask of your client, an accused person, to answer: "How did your interview process go?" And after the questions are asked of the accused person, you prepare your case.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Whether there is an advantage of actually having a video-recording, there will be questions that are asked if that recording of complainants of sexual offences, for example,is going to be substituted for the actual evidence in Court.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Moving on, Mr Speaker, I am looking at clause 42, which proposes section 166 amendments.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: At present, Mr Speaker, there is no further obligation on the defence to disclose the Supplementary Bundle of further information beyond what the prosecution gives.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The initial disclosure is by the prosecution and is to be reciprocated by the defence.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that this is the basis and thrust of a lot of the amendments on discovery that are being put forward by this Bill.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: If there is a requirement for the defence to disclose a Supplementary Bundle that arises from the premise that both the prosecution and the defence have the same starting point, that wish is for them to have a level playing field.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But the truth, Mr Speaker, is that resources are considerably different.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The prosecution has the resources of the state; the defence often has a team of very few lawyers.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I say this keeping in mind that the current practitioners of the Criminal Bar often are not pure practitioners of criminal justice.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Those practitioners have probably a considerable practice in civil litigation and arbitration, and, often, the criminal practice is done by the more senior practitioners of the Criminal Bar and is done pro bono or through Criminal Legal Aid Scheme (CLAS).

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: So, how would we even out then the playing field?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I ask this also because the prior assumption which was expressed by the Singapore High Court was to assume this natural imbalance, to know that the prosecution has the resources at its disposal, the defence definitely does not have the same resources, but may be inadvertently or by practice, prejudiced.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: They do not have the same number of people, they do not have the same investigation team.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: In the Singapore High Court case, this is what the Court observed.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The High Court said: "In an adversarial system of criminal justice, it is not the prosecution’s duty to assist the defence in making out a case nor is it appropriate to allow the defence to trawl through lists of unused material in the speculative hope of finding a defence, while placing the burden on the Court to decide on the relevance or credibility of those materials.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The prosecution’s overriding duty is to act fairly in the public interest and to assist the Court.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Surely, this does not mean it must be placed in the invidious position of having to assist the defence to this extent as well." That was the position that was taken in that case.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Allow me to conclude, perhaps, Mr Speaker, with a couple of points based on a recent case where I had the opportunity of seeing play out in Court.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I was not involved in this case but I attended the Court of Appeal hearings and I noticed an interesting point, and I say this in relation to perhaps section 394K that is being proposed in the Criminal Justice Bill.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: This particular section has already been raised by speakers before me and my hon colleagues rightly asked one question: does it go too far?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: So, if that is the test that is going to be applied, there are a couple of questions that arise.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Are there going to be certain terms that are going to be questioned again and again when we have a possibility of a miscarriage of justice?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: My hon colleague, Mr Kok Heng Leun, asked earlier whether if there is one try for a review, should that really prejudice or stop you from trying again.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: And I think the main idea is: will there be unfairness to the accused at any point?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: My hope is that the Court will be able to intervene at that point and say no.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: If we think we want to hear it, we will hear it.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But the question here is: are we tying the hands of the Court?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that we do not want to be inundated by unmeritorious claims.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But what if one of these claims turns out to undo or reverse an injustice?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Surely, there must be a possibility to bring that before the Court.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I compare this, therefore, to a particular recent case that I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The prosecution is currently appealing, so I will not go into the facts of this case since it is pending.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But what is concluded is a criminal motion that was put forward as to whether fresh evidence could be introduced.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It was a very tough case for the prosecution to argue.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The prosecution was trying to adduce fresh psychiatric evidence of a psychiatrist who had not actually examined the alleged victim.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: If that is the approach that we are taking, Mr Speaker, that the Court should be free, not handcuffed, by the words in the statute, will there be any change in this current position?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I ask this of the Senior Minister of State through you, Mr Speaker.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Criminal defence lawyers have a difficult but important role, Mr Speaker.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: That role is not popular, that role is often criticised, this happens even in this House.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: That as cross-examination is thought of and presented, the point is, people will ask, "If I do not ask a particular question, which is within the bounds, which is not insulting or outraging the modesty of a complainant or witness on the stand; if a particular question is not asked, will that somehow prejudice my client's case?" Again, I go back to Mohamed Ariffan’s case where that became almost a question that was raised; in this 2018 case.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It went on the level of questions that were asked at the trial below and whether a particular point remained a "live issue", or whether that particular point actually was concluded substantively such that the prosecution did not have the basis to raise it on appeal or if it was unavailable.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: All these are technical points but, again, I say it was a sexual offence case.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Since you have made your case, do not ask that question?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I do not think that should ever be the case, Mr Speaker.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Community sentences provide our Criminal Courts with alternative sentencing options.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They focus on rehabilitating rather than punishing the offender.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This proposed amendment is just one example, which indicates a more holistic and reformative approach to criminal justice.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There are instances in which the full brunt of society's condemnation of an offence must be brought upon a particular offender.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, it must not be forgotten that rehabilitation is aimed at changing the root causes of an individual’s criminal behaviour and should always be foremost in mind.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Moving forward, can I ask the Minister whether we will eventually let the Criminal Courts decide in which instances a community sentence can be imposed?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can I also ask if, in line with the spirit of these amendments, the Minister would consider providing our Criminal Courts with more alternative sentencing options?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A recent case illustrates the difficulties that Courts face because of limitations in sentencing options.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Judge will be releasing written grounds and what I will discuss is informed by media reports.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I do not, for one moment, suggest that the actions of this young offender should be minimised in any way.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: His actions have severely traumatised a young girl and she is likely to remain scarred for life.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What is notable from the press reports is the difficulty that the Judge faced with the limited sentencing options that were available.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this case, the defence lawyers had asked for reformative training.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The prosecution argued that the offender lacked the requisite cognitive abilities to understand the programmes because of his low IQ and was unlikely to benefit from reformative training.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am not sure though if this is the signal that we want to send out as a society when dealing with such an offender.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I would thus like to ask the Senior Minister of State if this concern can be addressed and whether we are looking into the sentencing options available to a Court faced with a young offender with some intellectual disability.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, on this Bill, I am supportive of the amendments to the victim compensation regime, which makes it easier for victims to obtain compensation through the criminal Courts, increase victim participation in the compensation order process and allow dependants to obtain compensation in certain cases.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The effectiveness of the regime will depend on how easy it is for victims and the dependants to navigate the process.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As such, can the Senior Minister of State elaborate on the procedures for seeking compensation from the criminal Courts?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can I also find out if there will be a limit on the compensation that can be ordered?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, can the Senior Minister of State clarify the rationale for limiting criminal compensation for a deceased victim’s dependants to funeral expenses and bereavement?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can she clarify further the rationale behind section 83(2), which departs from the current status quo where a woman is searched by a woman officer?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What checks will be in place to ensure that such searches are made with strict regard to decency as provided for under section 83(3)?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, lawyers have raised to me the concerns that the threshold for re-opening of criminal cases is too high, as fellow Members have raised previously.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The impetus behind instituting the review application framework seems to be to prevent the opening of floodgates to applications to reopen cases.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, it bears noting that when seen in the context of all the cases that go before the Court, the applications to re-open cases are few and far between.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While finality of proceedings is a key concern, ensuring that miscarriages of justice do not occur is as compelling a consideration.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State clarify that the new review application framework should not be interpreted to allow floodgates arguments to always prevail and that considerations of justice and the prevention of error should be given due weight, even at this late stage of the proceedings?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, I do welcome the introduction of video-recording for some Police interviews as it ensures greater transparency of the interview process.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It deters the use of coercive practices by investigators, deters false claims of involuntariness, assists judges in more accurately assessing the voluntariness and accuracy of statements made in custody and increases public trust in the Police.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, these benefits can only be achieved if proper safeguards are put in place.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Video-recording will only reduce instances of false confessions if it captures the entire interaction between interrogator and accused.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the words of Prof Michael Hor, "the purpose of such a scheme is defeated if the whole interrogation process spans across hours but only a portion of the statement or confession was recorded on tape".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Studies have shown that footage primarily focused on the suspect causes a "camera perspective bias" where viewers are given the notion that the statement was voluntarily given even when it was not.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Minister consider including in regulations or guidelines that the footage should have equal focus on both suspect and interrogator and, ideally, also shows the full extent of space in the room?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, for this point, I note that only rape under section 375(1)(a) has been listed as an offence for which statements must be video-recorded.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Vulnerable suspects are exceptionally vulnerable to giving false confessions and should be given special protection in the investigative process.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, this point relates in part to the rationale behind the Evidence (Amendment) Bill that victims of sexual and child abuse offences require special protection.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Aside from mitigating the trauma of the trial process on these particularly vulnerable victims, will the Minister consider enhancing the penalties or creating new offences where children are preyed on by online predators?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The ease of access and anonymity of the Internet heightens the susceptibility of children to exploitation by online predators.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, the Evidence (Amendment) Bill seeks to introduce a new section 154A to the Evidence Act to restrict two things: first, the questions that can be put to the alleged victim and, second, the type of evidence that can be adduced about the alleged victim.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first query relates to the types of questions that can be put to an alleged victim.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There is currently a provision in section 154 of the Evidence Act to prevent such questions from being asked of an alleged victim.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can I also clarify if the combined effect of section 154A(1)(a) and 154A(2)(c) is intended to stop questions before they are even asked?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If so, I am fully supportive of the amendment as the mere asking of a question is sometimes enough to provoke trauma in an alleged victim.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is lacking under section 154, which only prevents questions that have already been asked from being answered.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second question on the scope of sexual offences under the new section 154A is the types of offences that are considered sexual offences are set out in Part 2 of the new First Schedule.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: References there are made to several offences under the Penal Code and the Women's Charter.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Most of the offences referred to are capable, at first sight, of being considered of a sexual nature.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There are others which are not as clear.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, there is reference to section 356 of the Penal Code, which criminalises the assault or the use of criminal force to commit theft of property committed by a person.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While I can understand that, in certain cases, the prosecution prefers a charge under section 356 where sexual violence was used in the course of committing theft of property because of ease of proof, this also casts too broad a net as there may be other cases that do not involve violations of a sexual nature.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Criminal Justice Reform Bill and the Evidence (Amendment) Bill, taken together, introduces significant reforms to keep up with the evolving needs of our criminal justice system and the larger community.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The introduction of this Bill follows one of the most exhaustive reviews of the criminal justice system in recent history.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I commend the Government for involving the public and stakeholders, such as the Law Society of Singapore, in consultations before drawing up the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And we have just heard the account from the hon Nominated Member of Parliament Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan who stated his involvement as a consultant to one of the stakeholders in engaging the Government over several months.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The strength of this Bill is reflected in the consultative process that it underwent before reaching this House.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I take the opportunity to comment on three aspects of the Criminal Justice Reform Bill and two aspects of the Evidence (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I start with the proposed amendments in the Criminal Justice Bill to community-based sentencing.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As this House may recall, I had moved an Adjournment Motion some months ago to discuss the need for greater rehabilitative options to take into account the evolving needs of our sentencing regime, particularly for offenders suffering from mental disorders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As a result of these amendments, a whole new range of CBS options will now be open to the Court dealing with such cases.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I recall a recent appeal which I did before the High Court where parties were asked to consider if a short detention order in lieu of an imprisonment term – these are community sentences – may be imposed on a person who pleaded guilty to the offence of drink-driving causing a moderate level of harm to the person and property damage.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As a consequence, the person may lawfully state that he has no record of conviction.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This was the case for a company director who was convicted in January 2017 in the State Courts for failing to use reasonable diligence in the performance of his duties, an offence under the Companies Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Court imposed a short detention order of 14 days on him.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Upon serving the community sentence, he was able to move on with his life more easily as his job prospects were not indelibly affected.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This would not have been the case before the advent of the CBS regime.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Returning to my case, as a minimum sentence of fine was specified in the drink-driving provision, this option was not open to my client.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Now, depending on the circumstances of the case, the person may be imposed a short detention order.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This option will enable the Court to better tailor the punishment it imposes to the culpability of the offender.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It will not indelibly affect his employment prospects in the future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One further example of a CBS doing good for the person involved is a mother who was convicted for criminal intimidation against her own young children.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: At that point, she was suffering from clinical depression and other psychiatric conditions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As a result, the Order allowed her to continue with her treatment and the Child Protection Services allowed her to have supervised and, subsequently, unsupervised access with her children.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The result of it is that she has now reconciled with the children and she is well on her way to be back on her feet.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The enhanced CBS regime does not mean that we are going soft on crime.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It seems to me that more resources than ever before would be devoted to address the root causes of criminal conduct.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The significant difference here is that, under the enhanced CBS regime, we are in a better position to target root causes of criminal conduct by persons, especially those who have psychiatric conditions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The enhanced CBS regime will allow a wider class of persons to be subscribed to sophisticated rehabilitative programmes administered by duly qualified professionals, like in the case of the mother I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This will provide these persons with the best chance for rehabilitation, mend their ways and stop re-offending.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wholeheartedly support the proposed amendments to expand CBS and take the opportunity to make a few comments.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The present amendments do not alter the present framework for assessing an offender's suitability for a mandatory treatment order.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It, therefore, still remains that, under the CPC, the suitability assessment is conducted by a psychiatrist appointed by the Director of Medical Services of MOH.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my Adjournment Motion, I pointed out that there is a spectrum of mental disorders, some of which are easily treated, and others, such as personality disorders, which require sustained efforts to effect improvement.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, if the appointed psychiatrist makes a guarded prognosis of the offender's susceptibility to treatment and does not recommend an MTO, the Court would have no choice but to decline to make the MTO.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The effect of this is that the Court's determination of whether an MTO should be made is entirely reliant on the rigour and the professional opinion of the appointed psychiatrist.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is no mechanism for the Court to scrutinise the opinion of the appointed psychiatrist, for example, by reference to other independent psychiatric evaluation that the offender may have obtained, or through defence counsel's cross-examination of the appointed psychiatrist.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This approach is divergent from the approach taken in the context of reformative training.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Under the CPC, before an offender may be sentenced to reformative training, the offender would need to be assessed to be suitable for reformative training by a Singapore Prison Service psychiatrist.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In a Parliamentary Question that I had filed earlier this year, I had asked the Minister for Law whether it would consider expanding this requirement to allow for an independent report from a Court-appointed psychiatrist.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Minister's response was that the Singapore Prison Service psychiatrist is a professional who is familiar with the reformative training regime and would make his or her independent assessment of the offender.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Minister further highlighted that the Court may, if it deems necessary, direct that the SPS psychiatrist be cross-examined, or that further expert evidence or a second opinion be obtained, including from a Court-appointed psychiatrist.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, a point that I had raised in my Adjournment Motion was the approach taken to determine if an offender is "treatable" and, therefore, suitable for an MTO.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Then, I had highlighted that the UK has moved from a "treatability test" towards an "appropriate treatment test" when considering sentencing orders for offenders with mental disorders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The new test allows the UK Courts to make a detention order for treatment as long as, having regard to the nature and degree of the mental disorder and all other circumstances, the "appropriate medical treatment is available" for the offender.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As I recall, MinLaw agreed to study my proposal which, if accepted, will have the potential of extending MTOs to offenders who require more intensive treatment and rehabilitation regimes to cope with their psychiatric conditions and overcome their offending behaviour.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wonder if there is any landing reached on the study, please.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Next, another area of note is the proposed regulation of the use of psychiatric evidence in criminal proceedings.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The use of psychiatric evidence is an area of expert evidence that has seen some of the greatest growth in recent years.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The proposed amendments will require psychiatrists to be admitted to a Court-administered panel of psychiatrists before they are allowed to give expert evidence in Court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I do not see this amendment as singling out psychiatrists for stricter regulation than other types of expert witnesses.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: All experts must give evidence in an objective and professional manner.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On the contrary, the amendment recognises the prominent role that psychiatrists play in the criminal justice system.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Because so many cases turn on psychiatric evidence, it is important to ensure that such evidence in the form of opinions presented in Court is objective, well-researched and professional.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In view of the frequency with which psychiatric evidence is admitted in criminal cases, establishing a Court-administered panel is, in my view, a very good way to regulate such evidence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Could the hon Senior Minister of State please clarify whether it is contemplated that there will be a fixed quota of psychiatrists who are admitted to the panel?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Apart from the psychiatrists being qualified and having relevant work experience and character references, are there any other factors that the selection committee will take into account in determining whether to admit a psychiatrist to the panel?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I now move to another area of amendment to the CPC relating to the admissibility of statements taken by CPIB as evidence in non-corruption offences.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Section 27 of the PCA requires a person being interviewed in relation to offences under the PCA to give all information he is asked to give.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In contrast, for non-corruption offences, section 22 of the CPC preserves a person’s right against self-incrimination, by requiring a person giving a statement to the Police to state what he knows of the facts and circumstances, except that he need not say anything that might expose him to a criminal charge, penalty or forfeiture.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: At present, a statement given under section 27 of the PCA is inadmissible in relation to non-corruption offences.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This preserves the right against self-incrimination that is provided for in the Penal Code.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, the proposed amendments to section 258 of the CPC will change that, such that statements given to the CPIB under section 27 of the PCA, may now be relied on in non-corruption offences, when, ordinarily, if the statement were made to the Police, the right against self-incrimination would be preserved.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It will always be the case, for a person giving a statement to the CPIB under the PCA, to be legally obliged to say more than he would ordinarily say if interviewed by the Police in relation to a non-corruption offence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am struggling to identify a principled basis to preserve the right against self-incrimination in relation to non-corruption offences, which include serious white-collar crimes, such as criminal breach of trust as an agent while, at the same time, abrogating the right if the statement was originally given in relation to a corruption offence to a CPIB officer.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my view, the abrogation of the right against self-incrimination for PCA offences under section 27 of the PCA may be justified by reason of the nature of the corruption offences.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: At one level, these offences can be seen as "victimless" crimes because both the briber and the person receiving the bribes are likely to cooperate with each other and keep their conduct under wraps.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This makes such offences much more difficult to investigate.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Hence, the abrogation of the right against self-incrimination will allow the CPIB to be more effective in its investigation to tackle corruption.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, it is a different ballgame when the statements are used against a person for a non-PCA offence for which he would otherwise have a right against self-incrimination.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Could the hon Senior Minister of State please clarify what is the policy and rationale behind this dichotomy in treatment?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I noted earlier that the hon Member Ms Sylvia Lim expressed concern that the High Court making this determination sits in-camera.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I felt that sitting in-camera actually strikes a proper balance because, at that point in time, the Court would not have made a determination whether or not to sanction the DPA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is always a possibility that the case needs to go on and the corporation be prosecuted.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, in those circumstances, to make a pronouncement on what has happened in the proceedings may be sub judice, may even affect prosecution of the offences.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Therefore, I feel that the balance struck in the Bills by allowing the Public Prosecutor in a situation where the High Court gives its approval to make a public notice outlining the reasons for the High Court's decision is a good one.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this regard, the persons acting on behalf of the company in respect of the DPA would typically be the board of directors appointed by the shareholders to act on behalf of the corporation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, given that DPAs may have an impact on shareholder interests in the corporation, there may be times when shareholders’ interests may not be aligned with the position taken by the directors on behalf of the company, especially when the company is asked to pay fines of substantial sums.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As mentioned earlier, the DPA may provide for the appointment of an external monitor to monitor the corporation’s implementation of internal controls under the DPA or remediation, as the case may be, and to report to the prosecutor any misconduct in the implementation of internal controls.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is common in DPAs entered into with US authorities for such external monitors to be appointed at the corporation’s expense even though the monitor is, in reality, working for the prosecuting authorities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This structure has the potential of giving rise to a moral hazard, in that the external monitor may have a financial interest in having an expanded scope of work.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have seen real life examples of this.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have seen examples of monitors tying up the corporation’s business in knots, especially when the scope of monitoring has not been precisely determined and agreed to in the DPAs beforehand and submitting bills to corporations running into millions of dollars per month.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: While the contemplated DPA regime provides that the monitor is to report to the prosecutor any misconduct in the implementation of the corporation’s internal controls, it is not clear who has control over the monitor.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wonder if there is any intention to provide in the DPAs that the monitors be subject to oversight by the Court, akin to the position of liquidators appointed in the winding-up of companies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This would repose monitors with duties owed to the Court and ensure that his or her professional fees are fair and that the work done was properly within the scope of appointment under the DPA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I now turn to the proposed amendments to the Evidence Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Other countries have taken similar actions to protect victims of sexual offences from intrusive questioning in Court.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Pillai, you have half a minute to wrap up.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: However, I wish to seek some clarifications, given that the Evidence Act already contains restrictions on certain kinds of questions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: What is the rationale for having these restrictions dealt with in secondary legislation, instead of primary legislation?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: As I have pointed out, even the UK model —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: You do not have time for a last question.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Two of the changes proposed in this Bill involve the expanded usage of video facilities in legal proceedings.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Video link hearings have been successfully implemented since 1996 for bail and remand applications involving remandees.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Over time, video-link hearings were used for pre-trial proceedings, followed by first mentions in 2010.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Government then did not rule out that video link hearings would not expand into accepting pleas or sentencing.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I am glad to know that the state of technology has advanced such that it is possible to now hear more substantive matters like pleas of guilt and sentencing hearings in a more efficient, yet procedurally fair manner.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It also allows such matters to be heard without moving remandees between the Court and prisons.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This will reduce security risks, as well as the manpower needed for the management of risk.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While I support this proposed measure, I would like to ask the Minister what safeguards would there be to ensure that the usage of video link will not compromise on the standard and quality of the proceedings and the process of justice.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Will the various cybersecurity measures be in place to ensure that the links are free from being tapped or hacked by external parties?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Will there be consultation with stakeholders and Court users to ensure that the operational and technical aspects of the video-link hearings do not compromise the quality of justice?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How something is said is often as important as what is said.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I note that the Ministry has proposed a phased and measured approach.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is sensible, because too rapid an adoption of technology has its downsides.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: People, even seasoned media personnel, sometimes react differently when they know that there is audio-visual recording.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must not compromise on the effectiveness of our investigators, failing which, justice is then not delivered fairly for the victims as much as the suspects.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Time must be given to assess, calibrate and enhance the competencies of our officers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Appropriate training should be given to our Police investigators so that they can discharge the interviews fairly and effectively.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Court officers who are involved in such proceedings should also be trained to handle such recordings.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Some members of the public whom I have spoken to were concerned about the effectiveness of the video-recordings since.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As some Members of this House have also pointed out, there could be interrogation or interview before the actual recording.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In fact, some have also suggested more extensive recording and other processes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In my years of conducting investigations, I have never relied merely on confession or denial in the statement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our professional investigators look at the whole body of evidence surrounding a case.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must, therefore, never over-burden the investigation process with extensive SOPs, nor must we over-rely on video-recording when investigating and judging a case.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is imperative that the system provides conditions that make it easier for the cases to be reported.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Victims or complainants could be reluctant to report such crimes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must not allow sex fiends and child abusers to hide in the protection of open trauma and reluctance to report.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: When criminals capitalise on the anonymity and ease of communication and transaction that technology allows for, law enforcement agencies must be empowered to go after them effectively.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, facilitating access to computers situated outside of Singapore is critical in today's cross-border investigation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Otherwise, our laws would have failed to keep up with the changing environment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: At the same time, I hope that these enhanced investigative powers will be exercised with great care.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I am heartened to know that the stakeholders have been consulted and that their feedback has been taken into consideration.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With this, Mr Speaker, I support the Bill.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In November 2017, The Straits Times reported a burglary-rape case that the High Court passed sentence on.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In the case, a man broke into a house with the intention to burgle.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: When he saw the young victim in deep sleep alone in her bedroom, he decided to rape her and physically assaulted her by raining blows on her to beat her into submission and stop her resistance.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Following the traumatic ordeal, the High Court heard that the victim had become so fearful of people barging into her room that she now sleeps with the lights on and keeps a pair of scissors by her bedside.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The victim has been diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Following the breakup of her engagement due to the ordeal, she has thoughts that she is unworthy of others.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: She also blames herself for not sleeping in her grandmother's bedroom that night, thinking that she would not have been raped had she not slept alone that night.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In the sentencing of the case, Justice Chan Seng Onn told the perpetrator that words cannot fully express how much pain and suffering he had inflicted on the victim. "You have wrecked her life," said the High Court Judge.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I support and welcome the additions to the range of safeguards that currently exist.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Specifically, the disclosure of the victim's identity and having to recount a traumatic experience in the presence of the general public may not only be embarrassing, but traumatising and may undermine the individual's recovery process.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In some cases, the mere sight of one's attacker may deter the victim from testifying and cause more psychological trauma to the victims.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This can compromise the victim's ability to give their evidence in Court.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The Evidence (Amendment) Bill will allow the Minister to introduce rules about the type of questions that may be asked of the victim in Court.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This will help debunk the myth that the victim's dressing or behaviour somehow suggest that they consented to sex or that their report of a sexual offence should not be believed.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Legal counsel who abuse their position by posing insensitive questions which do not have any relevance to the case have been reprimanded by wise Judges in the past and I am, therefore, particularly heartened by the Evidence (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I remember reading about such a case recently.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: A lawyer was rapped by a District Judge when he suggested that it might have been the molest victim's dressing which increased the tendency for people to commit the sexual offence against her.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In other words, it was her fault that she was molested.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The Judge had then said that the lawyer's conduct had been completely unacceptable and fell short of expectations of lawyers.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: He had also noted that such questions are forbidden in Court under the Evidence Act and also proscribed under the Legal Profession Rules.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The Evidence (Amendment) Bill will, therefore, provide another layer of safeguards against hurting victims in Court.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This is a significant amendment as it is often the thought of going to Court and facing the defence counsel's cross-examination that is most daunting to the victims.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Instead, the examination of the victim is done in a private setting, away from the public eye.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This will help the victims recount their ordeal without causing more hurt and trauma.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: They are humane, compassionate and reflect a society that not only looks after, but is also respectful of the vulnerable members within.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Let us try and help the victims recover from their pain and move on with their lives.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In supporting this Bill, I will speak on three points: Vulnerable victims, expert witnesses, as well as vulnerable persons of unsound mind.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I concur with many of my colleagues who have spoken earlier, it is high time that we provide for appropriate restrictions on the kinds of questions and evidence that can be asked in criminal proceedings involving sexual offences or child abuse offences.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We recognise that our judiciary is impartial and can decide what is an inappropriate question to a witness, but, by then, the question may have already been asked.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Our legal profession is held in high regard, with only a very small minority of practitioners censured for inappropriate questioning, but, by then, the question may have been asked.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And so, there is still a role for safeguards because by the time an inappropriate question has been asked of a sex offence victim or a child abuse victim, it is too late to undo the psychological trauma caused to the person being cross-examined.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And so, we must avoid the risk that victims will be deterred and afraid of coming forward to give evidence because of the fear of being subjected to inappropriate questioning during cross-examination.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Victims of sexual abuse and child abuse have suffered terribly already.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We must avoid a situation where unnecessary additional suffering is visited upon the victims.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: These amendments and, in particular, the clarification of expert witnesses' duty to the Court, are very much welcomed because, as our society and justice system mature, expert evidence is increasingly sought to be introduced in legal proceedings, including criminal hearings.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For example, the use of medical evidence in criminal proceedings is becoming more commonplace, whether it is relating to the nature or cause of injuries; the mental state of the accused and its impact on the commission of an offence; or the possible explanations for, or the significance of, a substance that may be found in the blood or urine of an accused person.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, the creation of rules to regulate the giving of expert evidence will ensure that such testimony is held to strict as well as consistent standards and taken in an effective manner that would advance the pursuit of truth.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Indeed, the practice of "hot-tubbing" has been adopted in civil proceedings in Singapore for some time.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: As it involves the concurrent giving of evidence in an inquisitorial manner, "hot-tubbing" can reduce the time taken to take evidence from experts and also fosters a respectful environment where experts can put forward and have their opinions tested.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Currently, when a patient presents with a complex medical condition, a case conference may be convened.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Multiple experts from the same specialty may attend, or even multiple experts across multiple specialties.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In oncology, we call these conferences "tumour boards".

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Other medical specialties will have their own names for such conferences.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Such conferences are routinely held at reputable specialist centres around the world: Singapore, US, UK, Australia and so on.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is important to note that such case conferences are not adversarial by design.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Experts can ask questions or offer comments on other experts' views.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Clinical information is presented and discussed concurrently by a panel of experts.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Opinions can be tested or clarified, with the aim of seeking understanding of the scenario faced and what the range of appropriate decisions would be.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Sometimes, the discussion generates a range of opinions which the panel assesses to be within the bounds of what is appropriate.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: To clarify, I am not saying that medical case conferences are exactly the same as a "hot-tubbing" model of expert evidence in Court, but one might suggest that there are useful lessons which can be drawn.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, this review of how the Courts manage expert witnesses, especially medical expert witnesses, is to be welcomed.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It can help the Court arrive more swiftly at an understanding of evidence and what the key issues are, especially for medico-legal cases or where the medical evidence pertains to a criminal case.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Medical experts would also be able to discuss the evidence and provide opinions in an environment which more closely reflects the actual clinical decision-making and opinion formulating in day-to-day real world, responsible, expert practice.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This would also provide educational value for counsel as well as patient advocates.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But there are clarifications that we need to ask of the Minister.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I support the amendments which give the Courts and medical professionals a more prominent role in determining the most appropriate action to take in respect of persons who are found unfit to plead, or acquitted on the basis of unsoundness of mind.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Unfitness to plead or unsoundness of mind can span a spectrum of conditions.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Each case turns on its facts and it can be helpful to provide the Court with a range of options in dealing with such accused persons.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, we should welcome amendments which explicitly set out provisions that such persons can be released, if appropriate, to places such as a properly-equipped nursing home or other appropriate care facility.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This provides more options for dealing with such persons in a way that is humane while still serving the interests of justice, due process and protection of the public.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This is an important part of the proposed enhancements to procedural protections.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: They are part of an important shift towards a more progressive, more balanced, more modern criminal justice system.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is more so in an Asian society where a woman would be very embarrassed to relive the trauma that she had undergone.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Worse still is the fact that they could be cross-examined and asked questions which are very personal in nature and be dragged into a sort of exchange with another unknown person, namely the defence lawyer.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While I may not be legally trained, I know the defence in cross-examining a victim is trying his best to establish his client’s innocence, but, sometimes, these questions can be so cutting that they become more than an examination of facts relevant to the case.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the US, there was a case involving a student from Stanford who was accused of committing various sexual offences against an intoxicated victim.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: She was asked about her appearance, whether she drank alcohol and whether she had a history of cheating on her boyfriend.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In her victim impact statement, she recalled how badly the offence affected her and her ordeal of testifying in Court.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There was at least one occasion in Singapore where defence counsel had told the victim that he was going to ask her more insulting questions during her cross-examination.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This was right after she had informed him that she felt very offended when he had asked her to stand to assess how attractive she was.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In this case, the presiding judge had harsh words for the counsel.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Or would the presiding judge be consciously on the look-out for lawyers who pursue an irrelevant and salacious line of questioning?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If I may emphasise, it is important for the investigators to be fully conversant with procedures and protocols when taking DNA samples and other evidence.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have read of a number of cases where scientific evidence could not be tendered or were rejected because the lab tests could not be done or could not give any conclusive result because of certain lapses.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: From media reports, I recall this has happened in a few cases.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope that investigators follow the procedures very closely when collecting evidence.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With pre-recorded evidence, the time that a victim will have to spend in Court testifying will also be cut down.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There may be situations where the victim is very uncomfortable with giving a statement on video or is unable to recount the alleged incident accurately because he or she is traumatised.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What measures will be taken to ensure that victims are not disadvantaged by being made to give a statement on video in such situations?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Lastly, I note that the expansion of the community-based sentencing regime will mean that a greater number of offenders will be given access to rehabilitative opportunities.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This amendment is to be welcomed as it is a continued recognition of the fact that not all offences are best addressed through the traditional sentences of imprisonment and fines.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some offences may be committed in a moment of indiscretion and, thereafter, the offender may demonstrate a strong willingness and ability to be rehabilitated within the community setting.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There are some offenders who commit offences because they are unwell mentally.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Medical intervention, rather than punishment, should be the focus in such cases.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The expansion of MTOs as a sentencing option for more offenders and offences is thus a welcome change.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What is the criteria for determining the prescribed list for such offences?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The first is the protection for victims or complainants in sexual and child abuse offences.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The past few weeks, we have seen newspaper reports of serious sexual offences being committed against young people and even some shocking ones against older people.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: A common trend in many of these cases is that the victims are afraid of reporting the offence for a variety of reasons.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These include the stigma of being the victim of sexual abuse, the fear of both the perpetrator as well as the potential stress of going through the legal process and potentially having to relive the process once again in Court as the victim’s evidence gets challenged in the adversarial process.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As Court lawyers, we all know that a defence lawyer's job is to discredit the victims, so this creates a natural tension.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Some of these fears, the law cannot fully remove.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This includes allowing the victim to provide evidence by video although I think the details on how the adversarial system would preserve in this context are not yet available.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are also measures − interesting measures − to prevent the victim from seeing the accused in Court, including the provision of a screen, but this does not necessarily mean that the accused will not be able to instruct his lawyers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, again, it is to protect the victim.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are also procedures to hold part of the hearing in-camera, meaning out of the public eye, but not necessarily out of scrutiny of the adversarial process.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, I think there are well thought-through changes that will take away a lot of the stress the victim faces while, at the same time, giving the accused the opportunities he would need to challenge the evidence, as necessary, because, as some other Members have mentioned earlier, it is important that the accused is innocent until proven guilty.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But one must not underestimate the stress that victims face and I think there is a much broader societal cost to this as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One of the things that surprised many people, certainly myself, was the #me-too movement which came to life after the allegations against Harvey Weinstein.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And what was surprising was the number of prominent individuals who came forward to say they were victims of sexual abuse, but who had never themselves decided to make complaints prior to this or put themselves through the process.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: An even scarier case is that of Larry Nassar, the coach in the US who has been convicted of molesting young student gymnasts.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, this is really scary because these are conduct that could have gone unpunished and even unreported for years because victims were afraid to come forward.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, it is important for us to make sure that victims are not afraid to come forward.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The second aspect that I would like to talk about is DPAs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: DPAs are a work-in-progress in Singapore and it is interesting to add to the criminal process.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: DPAs are essentially agreements, I anticipate, most likely, with companies, to allow them to get an agreement not to be prosecuted now but to defer that if they cooperate.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, if a new management, for example, comes and takes over a company, it has two options.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The first option is to blow the whistle and expose the wrongdoing but, if they do that, there is a chance that the authorities may then prosecute the company.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The second option, of course, is to keep quiet and do nothing but that, of course, means the wrong may not go unpunished and that undermines the criminal process.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
