text: With the DPAs, this actually creates an interesting option for new management that comes in, because, in a sense, they are starting with a clean slate.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: They have the option to report the crime and discuss with the prosecution and try and get an agreement of this sort in place and exchange for cooperation in order to report on wrongdoings that had taken place before they had come.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, this, in a way, allows prosecution against the company to be deferred but, at the same time, for the wrongdoing to be investigated and for the wrongdoers to be taken to task.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This, I think, will be a powerful deterrent for potential wrongdoers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, if you just wanted the DPA as a sweet-heart deal, then that is not going to happen because there will be conditions set for this.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One risk that such agreements have is that they may be perceived as letting companies off the hook easily and this may create outrage, especially if some egregious corporate wrong takes place and the company is not punished because of the DPA.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: My own views would be that it would be important that, even if the DPA is in place but some serious wrongdoing has been done, some wrongdoers, preferably the key mastermind behind the wrongdoing, would be taken to task for this.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In England, Courts are required to give reasons.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Would the Senior Minister of State explain why Singapore has deviated from the English practice in this regard?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The third aspect – and this has been touched on by other Members earlier – it is the measures to prevent abuse of Court processes, particularly in relation to appeals.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In relation to appeals, there are two competing addresses.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: On the one hand, we want finality of the process.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, if a hearing has taken place and the Court has pronounced on it, the number of times you can re-open the case should be limited.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The countervailing consideration is, if important or material evidence comes up, say, after the conclusion of a hearing and, in criminal cases where this can have life or death affecting some cases, it will be important for a Court to be able to consider that.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Earlier, Members, including Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan, have mentioned, that the Kho Jabing case sets out these considerations in some detail.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: My own reading is that the current amendments are really codifications of what was set out by the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is important because it prevents abuse and makes it very clear that, in fact, appeals are exceptional.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, there is one clarification I would like to make on this.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And what happens, for example, if important new evidence becomes uncovered after this one additional chance is exhausted?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As the Senior Minister of State mentioned in her opening speech, this is a process that has been there for most criminal hearings where the prosecution has to set out that it has enough evidence to make its claim.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is generally a mechanism for the defendant to get out of having to go through a long protracted criminal process if they can establish upfront that the prosecution does not have much of a claim.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I understand, as some of the Members who spoke earlier have highlighted as well, that, in Singapore, the prosecution generally tends to be quite prudent in bringing forward actions and generally tends to get past this threshold without much difficulty.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This process tends to be just one that is an unnecessary process at the moment.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But notwithstanding the care which prosecutions are commenced, I would like to seek the Minister's assurance on one matter.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There are some clarifications or queries that have been raised and I would like to address them.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked how Police officers are being trained to take video-recorded statements.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Desmond Choo made a similar comment, whilst also suggesting training for Court officers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is vital for consistency in the way video interviews are conducted.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Sufficient officers have been trained to implement phase one.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As mentioned, the need to train officers in the skills and techniques needed to take video-recorded statements is one reason why VRI is being rolled out in phases.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Police will fine-tune the training programme, as they gain experience from the use of VRIs in phase 1.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As for other users of the system, such as Court officers, we will be engaging the relevant agencies to ensure that everyone is familiar with the new scheme before the first cases involving VRI enter the system.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Patrick Tay also asked about the safeguards put in place to ensure that the security of video-recorded statements is not compromised.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There will be safeguards in place to minimise the risk of loss of discs containing video-recorded statements.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan asked about copies of the videos and why they are not given to Defence Counsel and how many times the Defence will be able to view them.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The copies of the video-recorded interviews will not be handed over to Defence Counsel as video-recorded interviews may be leaked; or they may be lost or misplaced.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: A copy of the transcript of the recording would also be extended to the Defence during the CCD process and it was felt that an undertaking would not be sufficient for this purpose because, for example, there are some people who are unrepresented and an undertaking by an unrepresented accused person with no professional responsibilities may have a limited deterrent effect.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And if the worse happens and if, let us say, the video is leaked for some reason, punishing the lawyer or party responsible will not reverse the harm.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There are also the consequences of what happens if the video is distributed on the Internet because the impact is widespread.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The answer is that investigators should not be barred from asking leading questions because they are not legally trained and the procedural rules should not be introduced at this investigation stage where really the aim is to find out what happened.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Judge can view the recording and come to his or her own conclusions about reliability.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Kok Heng Leun was concerned that there should be sufficient safeguards to ensure the integrity of the video-recorded statements.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Much of the infrastructure is modelled on the best practices in other jurisdictions which are experienced in the use of VRI.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The technology adopted is also consistent with best practices to minimise litigation on the authenticity of the video statements.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, the rooms for VRI are purpose-built to ensure video statements are of good quality, both for sound and picture, while ensuring that other operations are not compromised.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These have been modelled on the purpose-built rooms used in Hong Kong for VRI.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng asked whether the Government would consider the use of video-recording in the preliminary interviews or other exchanges prior to the statement recording.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On a related note, Mr Kok Heng Leun expressed concerns about interactions between the Police and the suspect outside of the interview.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There would be various conversations between the Police and the accused persons from the time of arrest until statement taking and it would not be possible for officers not to have any conversations throughout.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, it would not be feasible to record every exchange that officers have with the accused person and, really, the primary intent of the interview is to take that person's statement.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, the video-recording will form the basis of the statement.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: By way of a convex mirror installed in the room, the full extent of the room can be observed in the camera.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The default angle to be used in Court, if any, would be the view focused on the interviewee, so that the demeanour of the interviewee may be seen in detail.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The overview may be shown as well, if so directed by the Court, for instance, to verify the accuracy of sign language interpretation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We are not closed to the idea of extending VRI further to more offences and to vulnerable suspects.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Infrastructure needs to be put in place, as I have mentioned, the purpose-built VRI rooms and even specially designed tables so that persons in the room cannot be obstructed from being seen on camera.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is, therefore, necessary that implementation will be done in phases to iron out whatever issues may become apparent and to ensure that there are adequate resources.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will consider this feedback as we expand the use of VRI in future phases.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked for clarification on the circumstances that a Police officer will take into account in deciding that a video-recorded statement should be taken, in cases where it is not mandatory to do so.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In deciding to exercise any power of investigation in the law, all criminal investigators generally consider the same factors and the ultimate aim is to advance the investigation, meaning to discover whether any criminal offence has been committed and the full facts of that offence, including those who committed it.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, in this context, it is not possible for me to give an exhaustive list but it would be a situation, I would assume, where the value of a video-recording would be high.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, if you have an accused with a mental disability, when you record a statement and you see the transcript, the way the answers come out may make a lot of sense but when you look at the person, the facial expression, the way somebody who is mentally disabled or has some cognitive disability is responding, that tells you another picture.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, that is an example of the sort of scenario where the investigator might decide in this particular instance, before we roll out other phases, to do so.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked for a clarification of how we will operationalise the video-recording of statements from victims.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will consider whether to require the recording officer to inform the victim from the outset that the statement would be used in a Court proceeding when we develop the details of implementation in consultation with stakeholders.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Kok Heng Leun asked about the timeline of implementation for video-recording of statements from victims.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There is a need to allow the law enforcement agencies sufficient time to train the investigation officers, to study the lessons of the pilot and then prepare the necessary facilities for VRI of victims.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Prosecution, members of the Criminal Bar and the Judiciary will also require time to acclimatise to the use of VRI evidence in Court.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As Mr Kok Heng Leun has pointed out, there are complexities involved in video-recording of statements from victims.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, we will, therefore, carefully monitor the first phase of VRI implementation before deciding how to operationalise video-recording of statements from victims.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked whether there will be a set of guidelines to assist Police officers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Police will develop their internal guidelines on this.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As mentioned, the use of video-recorded statements for victims will only be implemented in later phases because of the complex issues that I have highlighted.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Joan Pereira asked whether victims will be given a choice of whether to give a statement via video or in writing and Mr Kok Heng Leun asked a similar question.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, the victim’s willingness or level of comfort with giving a video-recorded statement will be an important factor.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, we will work again with the stakeholders to decide how best to operationalise this sensitively, before implementing it in future phases.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Joan Pereira also asked what measures will be taken to ensure that victims are not disadvantaged if they are unable to recount the alleged incident because he or she is traumatised.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Victims can indicate their preference not to give their statements on video if they are uncomfortable with it.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For sexual crime victims, their cases are handled by specialist investigation officers who are trained in victim care.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked a question not exactly in relation to VRI, but related – whether we should review the rule which allows for a statement made to a Police officer ranked Sergeant or above, to be admitted in evidence.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: While there may be more officers, including newer officers, who hold at least the rank of Sergeant today than before, it would be mistaken to take that as a lowering of the standards expected of officers of that rank.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Police have rigorous training programmes and internal guidelines in place to ensure that anyone with the rank and authority to take statements does so with the highest level of competence and professionalism.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Next, I move on to the computer-related powers of investigation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Desmond Choo supported the enhanced powers but expressed the hope that they would be exercised with care.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Police will take into account the nature of the cases and the requirement for the information, before issuing any order under section 39.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng asked for clarification of the rationale behind the amendment which allows a male officer to search a woman suspected of a terrorist act and what safeguards there are to ensure that searches are made with strict regard to decency.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There is a well-recorded history of the use of women in terror attacks.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Some have been coerced into this role, but others have volunteered.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: One of the earliest users of this tactic was the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) or the "Tamil Tigers", in their campaign against the Sri Lankan government.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They assassinated former Indian Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi in a suicide bomb attack in 1991.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Tragically, this is not a phenomenon of the past.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The BBC very recently reported that Boko Haram in Nigeria has been kidnapping girls, some as young as 13 and forcing them to go on suicide bombing missions in crowded public areas.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This was confirmed by some girls who managed to escape.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Research suggests that terror groups use female attackers to gain specific tactical advantages.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These include a perceived unwillingness on the part of security officers to search women.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In Iraq, Al-Qaeda repeatedly exploited a cultural taboo against the searching of women, allowing their female suicide bombers to pass through checkpoints without being searched.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, it really is about striking a balance.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, the officer must reasonably suspect that the woman is involved or has involvement in a terrorist act.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Second, the officer must believe in good faith that the terrorist act is imminent.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Third, the officer must believe in good faith that the search cannot be made within a reasonable time by a relevant officer who is a woman.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The rationale, as explained, is that time is of the essence in such situations and it is where any delay could mean loss of lives.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Police will put in place strict Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) to ensure that the searches are made with strict regard to decency.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked whether the prohibition against indemnity agreements would make it unduly difficult for families to raise bail monies, as they sometimes need to get contributions from relatives and friends.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The prohibition against indemnity agreements is premised on the seriousness of a surety's duty.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The serious nature of this duty has been emphasised by the Courts on various occasions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, the High Court reiterated in a case last year that sureties' obligations were of "cardinal importance" and "consequences of significant gravity" must, therefore, attach to any breach of such obligations.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is, therefore, important that we do not allow sureties to be indemnified by third parties, as doing so would remove the incentive for them to fulfil their obligations.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Having said that, I should clarify the scope of the offence.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It will require that the surety enters into an agreement with the third-party, that if bail is forfeited because the accused person absconds, the third-party will cover all or part of the forfeited bail that the surety will be liable to pay.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It does not mean that the surety can never borrow money to raise bail.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, if the surety borrows some money to raise bail and remains liable to repay that money, then it is not an indemnity.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In other words, the surety must have a vested interest in ensuring that the person turns up in Court.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked for statistics on the frequency of bail granted and the incidence of absconding in the past five years.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He also asked whether such persons were later apprehended and how they were dealt with.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Criminal practitioners would know that bail is granted in the vast majority of cases.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Notwithstanding the recent high-profile case, absconding from bail is also rare.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: When accused persons on bail abscond, the bail sum pledged by the surety may be forfeited.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If the accused person is still within Singapore, attempts will be made to locate and arrest them.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In the event that the accused person flees overseas, Police may issue an INTERPOL Red Notice.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Police forces in INTERPOL member states will then help to locate and arrest the accused person.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The wanted person may then be extradited back to Singapore.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Absconding from bail is also an aggravating factor which could result in a higher sentence when the accused person is later brought back to face charges against him.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The changes made to the CPC in this Bill will further strengthen our bail regime.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Patrick Tay also asked about the rationale behind allowing bail for extradition cases where special circumstances apply and what such special circumstances would be required to grant bail in such cases.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We thought that it would be too harsh to prohibit bail in extradition proceedings without exception.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The specific "special circumstances" which would justify the grant of bail will be prescribed in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, for example, special circumstances could exist if the accused person was a juvenile, or was sick or infirm.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I move on now to enhancing protection for victims of sexual and child abuse.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I am very heartened that so many Members have stood up to support the proposals on enhancing protection for victims of sexual and child abuse.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Kok Heng Leun related a particularly moving story about the impact on a victim and many of the other Members, too, have cited examples.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This just goes to show how much impact Court procedures can have on a victim and how they can sometimes be forced to relive over and over again the dreadful experience that they first underwent.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, it is very important that we have to address this.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Patrick Tay pointed out some myths and stereotypes which may be associated with sexual offences.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And while not all of them can be addressed through legislation, the present amendments do go some way towards tackling them.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, Mr Patrick Tay asked whether sections 366 and 367 of the Penal Code could be included in the First Schedule of the Evidence Act.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Sections 366 and 367 of the Penal Code are offences of kidnapping or abduction albeit with a sexual element.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That said, the First Schedule gives us the flexibility of including other offences where it is determined that restrictions should similarly apply.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Patrick Tay also asked whether more offences, such as those for criminal intimidation or harassment, should be given the same treatment.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In particular, he is concerned about instances where the criminal intimidation imputes unchastity to a woman or where harassment is sexual in nature.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He asked whether the judge ought to be given the flexibility to decide to apply similar restrictions on cross-examination, even though they are not offences listed in the First Schedule.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The restrictions on cross-examination are intended to apply to those sexual offences where questions relating to the victim's sexual behaviour, sexual history and the physical appearance are most likely to be asked.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For other offences, such as criminal intimidation or harassment, the Evidence Act gives the judge the power to disallow certain forms of cross-examination.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, as a starting point, only relevant questions can be asked on cross-examination.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And the Court has the power to disallow questions that are intended to insult or annoy.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Indecent and scandalous questions may also be forbidden.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan asked whether the restrictions will create a chilling effect on Defence Counsel which will make their difficult job even harder.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The answer is that, actually, all that is required is for leave to be sought in advance.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, so long as the Counsel can show that it is relevant and that there is a good reason for it, leave should be granted and leave will be granted if it is in the interest of justice.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, we are not saying that the topic cannot be raised but you must show a very good reason why you are asking those questions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We are aware of the various operational issues that may arise and we will work closely with stakeholders on implementation, to ensure that the use of the screen is not counter-productive.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng has asked whether the Government will also consider enhancing penalties or creating new offences, especially for online predators.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The area of sexual offences is one area that we are looking at.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These recommendations will include recommendations on whether penalties should be enhanced and whether new offences are needed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng also sought a clarification on what questions the proposed section 154A(1)(a) of the Evidence Act will cover that do not already fall under the scope of section 154 today.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On a related note, Mr Louis Ng asked whether the combined effect of the new section 154(1)(a) and section 154(2)(c) is intended to stop certain questions even before they are asked.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The specific restrictions will be set out in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Hence, unlike section 154, which is broadly phrased in terms of the questions that are forbidden, section 154A will be more specific.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As Mr Louis Ng has pointed out, the requirement for prior leave is also a key difference between section 154 and section 154A.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This will ensure that only appropriate questions that are in the interests of justice may be asked.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The leave stage will also insulate victims from hearing insulting and irrelevant questions, as the Court will not permit such questions to be asked.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The restrictions will only apply if the accused or Defence seeks to ask questions relating to the victim's sexual behaviour.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If these types of questions are asked in the context of an offence under section 356, then the restrictions may apply.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Section 356 has been included because victims of such offences have always received the benefit of certain protective measures, such as being able to give evidence via video link.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: To have taken them out would also mean that a class of victims that were previously given the benefit of protective measures would now be deprived of the new protections.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, even after this legislation, we will continue to review the classes of victims that will be covered by various protective measures to ensure that the correct balance is struck.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Joan Pereira asked what recourse a victim has, if she felt that the counsel had ridiculed her to the point of disparaging her reputation during a Court hearing and whether the presiding judge would consciously be on the look-out for irrelevant insulting questions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As we have seen in previous cases, lawyers who cross the line may be subject to disciplinary proceedings.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Judges are also vigilant to ensure that questioning by Defence Counsel does not cross the line.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The fact that the Court can control the questions before they are asked, in the absence of the victim, is significant.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This gives the Judges more control over the proceedings to ensure that the victims are not intimidated by insulting and irrelevant lines of questioning.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Joan Pereira also mentioned that it is important for investigators to handle DNA samples and other forensic evidence carefully.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Should any mishap occur – which, hopefully, they would not – the relevant agencies will conduct internal investigations and make improvements to their protocols where needed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I move on now to the Enhancement and Rationalisation of Fitness to Plead and the Unsoundness of Mind regime.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is just that the criminal charge element is removed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: A person confined under the Mental Health (Care and Treatment) Act is periodically reviewed and assessed for his or her suitability for release.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I move on now to Deferred Prosecution Agreements (DPAs).

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked whether the requirement for corporate offenders to be represented by counsel includes in-house counsel.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The legislation states that the party must be represented by an advocate, which is defined as an advocate and solicitor lawfully entitled to practise criminal law in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Having said that, in-house counsel who do not fall into this category can assist or participate in negotiations on the DPA.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And when you go to Court, you would have to be somebody who has the right of audience.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked whether a code of practice for the use of DPAs, similar to that published in the UK, will be published here.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The publication of the code of practice in the UK is consistent with their general position that prosecutorial guidelines are published.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked for a confirmation that the legislative framework on DPAs does not preclude the Court from allowing interested stakeholders to join in the proceedings.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, the basic position should be that a company's decision-making power lies with its board.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Other stakeholders, such as shareholders, do not have the same power.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Courts have actually pronounced on the reason for this.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The reason is that the board and the directors have a fiduciary duty.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They are obliged to act in the best interest of the company.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Shareholders do not have a similar fiduciary duty.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Shareholders are free to act in their own interest.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, in some cases, their interests may well be aligned, but, sometimes, they may not be.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: At the end of the day, when you are entering into a DPA and negotiating it, the primary decision-making power should rest with the company and its board.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If the shareholders have issues with the decisions, then they have other avenues available to them, such as the General Meeting, and, of course, the other rights available to shareholders under the Companies Act.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is open to the Court to ask for information about the possible impact of a DPA on various stakeholders, to assist in making its decision on the approval of a DPA.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Murali Pillai also proposed that monitors appointed under a DPA be subject to oversight by the Court.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The conditions that can be attached to a DPA are deliberately left flexible, subject to the High Court's approval.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is open to parties to negotiate and set out details concerning the role and supervision of monitors in the DPA.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Patrick Tay, Mr Vikram Nair and Ms Sylvia Lim asked why the High Court is not required to give reasons in a DPA decision.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Sylvia Lim also asked why DPA proceedings in the High Court would be held in camera.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We considered that if proceedings for a DPA approval were held in the public view and, if the DPA did not eventually come into force, the company negotiating the DPA would be prejudiced, or could be prejudiced, in any future criminal proceedings based on the same facts – that was actually the point that Mr Murali Pillai made.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Because if companies have reason to fear that their willingness to negotiate a DPA will prejudice their defence later on, then they may be unwilling to volunteer information or cooperate and the benefits of the DPA scheme will then be undermined.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That is the same reason that representations written by the Defence to AGC are protected by the "without prejudice" privilege.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is essentially the same underlying philosophy that applies to "without prejudice" negotiations.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With respect to the other question of why we do not require the Courts to give reasons, some of it relates to this, but the general thinking is this: the DPA is not a judgment.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, it does not have a binding effect; stare decisis does not apply.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It does not set a precedent for other DPAs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Under these rules, the Court is not prevented from giving grounds.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In other words, the system that we have is actually consistent with the current system that we have for any other type of judgment whether it be criminal or civil, meaning that our Courts are not under a compulsory obligation to publish grounds, certainly at first instance.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If it goes on appeal, it is different because, obviously, in an appeal, you are looking at the reasons why the judge decided in a particular way and you need the grounds for decision.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Currently, for criminal and civil proceedings, Courts sometimes give grounds – they sometimes give oral grounds, sometimes they give written grounds.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is open to the Court to give grounds if the Court wishes to do so, but there will also be some cases which are actually very straightforward and it is not necessary for the Court to give written grounds.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, we essentially leave it to the Courts and the Courts can decide where it may be appropriate to do so.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I am aware, of course, that, in the UK, they give grounds but there are other jurisdictions where DPA is applicable where they do not, such as the US, for example.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So we thought we would just have a system that is consistent with the current practice on judgments.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Moving on to the Criminal Procedure Rules Committee (CPRC).

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Patrick Tay proposed that the CPRC should seek inputs from social science and technology experts.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The CPRC will consult the relevant stakeholders, where appropriate.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On abolition of Committal Hearings, Mr Vikram Nair asked for an assurance that with the replacement committal hearings with the transmission procedure, there would still be sufficient safeguards to filter out unmeritorious prosecutions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As mentioned, the key benefit of committal hearings, as practised today, is pre-trial documentary disclosure of the prosecution's case.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: At trial, the Defence is free to cross-examine the prosecution's witnesses.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If at the end of the prosecution's case there is no prima facie evidence of guilt, the accused will be acquitted without being called upon to raise a defence.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This threshold, together with the CCD process, provides the answer to Mr Vikram Nair's question.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This move will actually benefit accused persons in reducing their time spent in remand or waiting for the trial to commence, as well as the overall administration of justice.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In short, basically, the Committal Hearing procedure before had two main advantages.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: One is disclosure, or discovery, and second is the cross-examination.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: You still get a chance to cross-examine when it goes on to a High Court trial.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The benefit is that you shorten the time the person spends in remand.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I move on now to the video-link hearings.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Desmond Choo asked what safeguards will there be to ensure that the usage of video link will not compromise on the standard and quality of the proceedings and will not affect the process of justice; whether cybersecurity measures will be in place to ensure that the links are free from being hacked by external parties; and whether there will be consultations with stakeholders and the Court users.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Careful consideration has been given to ensure that the fairness of the hearing process is not affected by the use of video link.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have and will continue to engage with the Criminal Bar and other stakeholders on the implementation of this scheme.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The necessary security measures will be considered in the technical part of the planning and implementation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Sylvia Lim expressed some concerns about whether allowing video-link proceedings for guilty pleas and sentencing proceedings will diminish the impact of warnings from judges.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: One of the reasons we are extending video-link hearings to more substantive matters at this time is improvements in technology.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will be using video-link technology with sufficient audio and visual fidelity so that the Court proceedings will not be adversely affected.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is actually part of the overall general move.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We think that, going forward, technology is going to be more and more infused in practice, both civil as well as criminal.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That is the direction in which it is moving.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Sylvia Lim was also concerned with confidential communication between defence counsel and their clients.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We had consulted the Law Society and the Criminal Bar and they, too, had raised this point and we have had discussions with them.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Obviously, the confidentiality is protected as well and that has been working reasonably well.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: From past experience and based on our conversations with the Bar, we think there is a consensus that with the right technology and processes, we can have systems for communications that will satisfy the requirements of the Defence.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In short, we will continue to consult the Criminal Bar on the implementation in this respect but the important thing will be to ensure the confidentiality and that the solicitor-client privilege is preserved.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In essence, currently, there is already a system for counsel to speak to the accused and to take instructions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng asked about the kind of subsidiary legislation that we envisage for regulating expert evidence and whether there will be consultation on the proposed regulations.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The answer is, yes, there will be consultation with relevant stakeholders.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: One example of subsidiary legislation that we envisage, as Dr Tan already alluded to, is to expressly state the obligations of an expert witness, as is currently done for civil procedure.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Patrick Tay, Mr Christopher de Souza, and Mr Kok Heng Leun, all asked whether there are safeguards to ensure a sufficiently wide choice of psychiatrists.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The selection criteria has not been finalised yet.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is not the intention to set an extremely high bar for admission to the panel; we expect that most psychiatrists with the relevant forensic training will be able to qualify.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They will be drafted to ensure that there is a sufficient pool for psychiatrists.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: MinLaw welcomes any feedback as we work through how to formulate the criteria.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This should also deal with Mr Kok Heng Leun’s concern as to whether it will be more costly to hire a psychiatrist.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Given that we expect the impact on the choice of psychiatrists to be minimal, it should not become more expensive for the accused person to hire a psychiatrist.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Kok Heng Leun expressed concern that a psychiatrist on the panel may be unwilling to state honest but controversial views.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The proposal is not intended to target psychiatrists who give unconventional views.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is intended to target psychiatrists who display a clear lack of objectivity or competence.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: A psychiatrist will not be removed from the panel just because the Court does not accept his or her opinion.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We also note Mr Patrick Tay's suggestion to provide the panel of psychiatrists with training.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will be working with stakeholders to see what needs they have in this regard.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked whether there will be a fixed quota of psychiatrists.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Murali Pillai also asked for elaboration on what other factors the selection committee will take into consideration in deciding whether to admit a psychiatrist to the panel, besides qualifications, work experience and character references.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As mentioned, the selection criteria have not been finalised; so, we will work with stakeholders on suitable criteria.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If Members, especially those in private practice, have thoughts on this, they should feel free to send their feedback to MinLaw.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked about the clarification on the policy and rationale behind making statements recorded under section 27 of the PCA, admissible in respect to non-PCA offences.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Under the current law, therefore, what might happen is that a person, in the course of being investigated for corruption, may reveal that he or she has also committed another offence.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The CPIB will then have to go through the artificial exercise of recording another statement under the CPC.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And then, what happens if in the second statement, the accused person changes his tune and decides not to reveal the fact of such an offence?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Should the accused person be allowed to avoid prosecution on the procedural ground that section 27 PCA statements cannot be admitted in prosecution for other offences?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The real concern, then, is whether this amendment will create an incentive for CPIB officers to circumvent the privilege against self-incrimination in the CPC.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked for clarification on whether the change to the admissibility of section 27 PCA statements is a clarification or a change in the law.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The explanatory statement uses the word "clarify" because the relevant Court decision states that in respect of non-corruption offences, "the failure to inform the person interviewed of his privilege against self-incrimination, coupled with telling him that he is legally bound to tell the truth may amount to an inducement".

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This leaves it debatable in each case whether merely telling a person that he is bound to tell the truth amounts to an inducement.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, this clarification is achieved through a substantive change.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Courts will not be allowed to treat the mere fact that a CPIB officer told the interviewee that he is bound to tell the truth under the PCA, as grounds that the statement was given under an inducement for the purposes of a non-corruption offence.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Joan Pereira asked about the up-take rate of CBS.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Since 2011, the number of offenders who were sentenced to community sentences has varied from around 100, to more than 200 offenders.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will continue to work with stakeholders to encourage the use of community sentences in suitable cases.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked for statistics on MTOs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Given that MTOs, along with the various other community orders, have been introduced relatively recently, we have limited data on recidivism.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Patrick Tay also asked what safeguards are put in place to ensure that victims of offenders placed on MTOs are protected while the offender is receiving treatment in the community and he cited the case of a woman who continued harassing her neighbour despite being on an MTO.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Court is unlikely to impose an MTO where there is clear evidence that the accused person is likely to cause danger to others while remaining in the community.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In such cases, the principle of prevention is likely to outweigh the principle of rehabilitation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Court may also impose conditions as it thinks fit to mitigate the risk of harm to the victim.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We are also enhancing the MTO regime to allow for more flexibility of the treatment programmes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, we are empowering the Court to order a period of inpatient treatment for cases which require more intensive treatment.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ultimately, we have to accept that there is some risk created when imposing a community sentence but this must be weighed against the alternative, which is likely a relatively short sentence of imprisonment.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If the root causes of offending are not addressed, the offender has a high chance of re-offending upon release, especially if the cause is mental illness.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Joan Pereira asked for an indication of the kinds of more serious offences that will be prescribed, to render them eligible for MTOs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Offences that reflect a danger to public safety or which require greater deterrence will not be prescribed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Murali Pillai raised two points, which he also raised earlier in an Adjournment Motion on CBS.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, he observed that the Court cannot take a different view from the appointed psychiatrist, as regards an offender’s susceptibility to treatment.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He also cited a previous case that he dealt with, where an apparent change in opinion on the part of the appointed psychiatrist, resulted in the Court being unable to impose an MTO on the accused person.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We had checked on this with IMH following the Adjournment Motion in September last year.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The psychiatrist in question explained that his first report had indicated that while a period of inpatient stay may be beneficial in his condition, the likelihood of significant improvement in his condition with treatment was very low.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The report was not for the purposes of assessing MTO suitability.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The second report, some four months later, was for the purposes of assessing MTO suitability.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In the second report, the psychiatrist concluded that the offender was, in fact, not suitable for MTO as the treatment available was not likely to result in significant improvement in his condition.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I hope that this clarifies the situation that Mr Murali Pillai raised.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Murali Pillai’s broader point, however, is that the Courts should be allowed to impose an MTO, notwithstanding the appointed psychiatrist’s opinion that the offender is not suitable for MTO.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The reasons for not taking up this suggestion are as follows.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The current position, therefore, aligns the diagnostic and treatment elements of MTOs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As regard Mr Murali Pillai's point on the difference between the MTO regime and the RT regime, there is, in fact, no inconsistency.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In the context of a RT pre-sentencing report, the psychiatrist is focused on whether there is any aspect of the offender’s mental condition that renders him or her unsuitable for RT.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, the psychiatrist will take into account whether any condition will be aggravated by the RT environment, or whether it will affect his or her ability to be rehabilitated in the RT environment.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If the psychiatrist does not find any reason to recommend that an offender is unsuitable for RT, and the Court finds, after considering all relevant factors, that the offender should be sentenced to RT, the end result is that the offender will be sentenced to RT.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The offender is not sentenced to undergo mandatory treatment for a psychiatric condition.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The ethical issue highlighted above does not, therefore, arise in the context of RT pre-sentencing reports.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked for an update on the Ministry's consideration of his proposal made at an Adjournment Motion some time back, on moving towards a different test for determining MTO suitability.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng asked whether we intend to eventually allow the Courts the full discretion to decide when a community sentence can be imposed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have taken a balanced approach in deciding which offences and offenders should be eligible for community sentences.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Some crimes may be too serious and it would not serve the justice system well to allow such offenders to be given community sentences.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Some offenders may not benefit from community sentences.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Hence, the regime is carefully calibrated and we need to draw the line somewhere.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Nevertheless, we will continue to examine the eligibility requirements and extend the line, where appropriate.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked whether we will consider giving the Courts more alternative sentencing options.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He asked this in the context of a recent case where reformative training was imposed on a young intellectually-challenged offender for the sexual assault of a 16-year-old girl.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng asked for elaboration on the process of ordering victim compensation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked a similar clarification on whether this changes the existing principle that the Court should not be required to embark on complicated investigations of fact or law when deciding on compensation orders.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The key procedures and the processes involved will be found in the CPC Rules, after consultation with the relevant stakeholders like AGC and the Courts.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have already been consulting these stakeholders to ensure that the processes and procedures implemented will be simple and inexpensive.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That said, compensation orders of a certain amount can only be made by the Criminal Courts if there is sufficient and cogent evidence to support the amount being ordered.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In addition, our Courts have previously said that a compensation order should not be oppressive and the Court must be satisfied that the accused either has the means available, or will have the means, to pay the compensation within a reasonable time.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is to ensure that the compensation order does not simply become a de facto extension of imprisonment, which may be unfair to the offender.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked about the rationale for limiting criminal compensation for a deceased victim’s dependants to funeral expenses and bereavement.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, compensation for bereavement has been pegged to a fixed quantum set out in the Civil Law Act.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: More complex forms of damages arising from the death of a person, such as loss of amenity or loss of future earnings, should be dealt with in the Civil Courts.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I move on now to the question of abuse of process in concluded criminal cases.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng expressed some concern about the threshold for re-opening a concluded criminal case.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He asked that considerations of justice and the prevention of error be given due weight even at that late stage of the proceedings.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Kok Heng Leun raised a similar concern.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I believe Asst Prof Mahdev also highlighted this.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The re-opening procedure, including the relevant threshold tests, is largely a codification of a number of considered decisions made by the Court of Appeal in balancing the interests of finality against the need to prevent a miscarriage of justice.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We are confident that in administering the threshold tests, which the Court had itself developed in case law, the Court will give due regard to the prevention of miscarriages of justice.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Government shares this concern and that is why this procedure is being legislated.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It may be helpful to look at the provisions in the amendments.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In terms of looking at the requirements for the exercise of the power of review, there are a few things that have to be taken into account.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, the applicant in the review application must satisfy the appellate Court that there is sufficient material on which the appellate Court may conclude that there has been a miscarriage of justice.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The key thing here is miscarriage of justice and that material must satisfy the following requirements.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Before the filing of the application of leave to make the review application, the material must not have been canvassed at any stage of the proceedings in the criminal matter, in respect of which the earlier decision was made.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, it must be remembered that this scenario is different from a scenario where something is coming up for consideration for the first time.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is intended to address the scenario where it has been heard once – it has been appealed, it has been heard – and, therefore, you are trying to re-open it again, which means the Court has already applied its mind.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: You, therefore, have to show that it is something where it could not or had not been canvassed at an earlier stage.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Because if it had been canvassed at an earlier stage and it was considered and the Court had said no, then really, it should follow the normal procedural rules, which is, that you do not re-open concluded hearings.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is also a requirement that even with reasonable diligence, the material could not have been adduced in Court earlier.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For the purposes of the subsection on what is demonstrably wrong, it must be shown that the decision was based on a fundamental misapprehension of the law or the facts, thereby resulting in a decision that is blatantly wrong on the face of the record.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In short, the underlying philosophy of this is that you already have had several chances at it and the Court has considered it, not once, but twice, or possibly more.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And if you want to overturn this, you must show that there has been a miscarriage of justice or it is very, very clear the earlier decisions were wrong.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But, of course, people may ask: but what if there is one case where actually something turns up which was not considered before and it is demonstrably wrong, you think it is miscarriage of justice, but it is does not meet one of these conditions?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Fundamentally, what Courts seek to do is to do justice.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Obviously, I would not anticipate what the Courts would do but I can say that if it is very, very clear to a Court that there has been a miscarriage of justice and something is really fundamentally and really wrong which could not have been addressed earlier, then the Court has its inherent power to review the matter.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think I have addressed most of the queries except possibly for one question by Asst Prof Mahdev which is on requiring the defence to disclose a Supplementary Bundle and what should be done to balance the difference in resources between the defence and the prosecution.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And such adjournments would actually lengthen the proceedings.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Other than that, I think I have addressed the various queries.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I wonder whether the learned Senior Minister of State has a response to my query in relation to why we are taking the secondary legislation route as opposed to the primary legislation route, especially since the broad contours of the proposal on how to protect the victim of child abuse or sexual offence from witness' trauma and how a balance be struck in relation to ensuring the accused's right to a fair trial is not prejudiced.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It is already kind of spelt out in the hon Senior Minister of State's speech.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Also, would it not be better for at least broad rubrics of the policy intent to be provided in the primary legislation so that we can ensure that the rules issued thereunder would be consonant with the policy intent?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Lastly, would it not be a better alternative to allow such rules to be determined by the newly proposed Criminal Procedure Rules Committee as opposed to the Minister?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This will allow the judicial inputs to be obtained in the making of any such rules.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Murali Pillai sought clarification on why the restrictions on asking certain kinds of questions of victims of sexual offences or child abuse are being contained in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Murali Pillai also suggested that if the subsidiary legislation had been made in this area, it should be determined by perhaps the CPRC and not the Minister.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is so that the Court would be able to give input on the nature of the restrictions.
